requirements.canonical: A module IS the top-level unit of TTCN-3.
A module CANNOT be structured into sub-modules.
A module MAY import definitions from other modules.
A module MAY have module parameters to allow test suite parameterization.

A module IS a set of definitions of test components, communication ports, other kinds of types, constants, templates, functions including the module control function, signatures for procedure calls at ports and test cases.
The module control function calls the test cases and controls their execution.
The module control function MAY declare local variables.
Program statements (such as if-else and do-while) CAN be used in the module control function to specify the selection and execution order of individual test cases.
Global variables ARE NOT supported in TTCN-3; a variable SHALL NOT be declared directly in the module definitions part.
TTCN-3 predefined basic types include integer, float, boolean, verdicttype and the string types.
TTCN-3 structured types include record, set, union, enumerated and map types and arrays.
A template IS a special kind of data structure that provides parameterization and matching mechanisms for specifying test data to be sent or received over ports.
The operations on ports provide message-based and procedure-based communication capabilities.
Procedure calls MAY be used for testing implementations which are not message based.
Dynamic test behaviour IS expressed as test cases.
TTCN-3 program statements include behaviour description mechanisms for alternative reception of communication and timer events, interleaving and default behaviour.
TTCN-3 supports test verdict assignment and logging mechanisms.
A TTCN-3 language element MAY be assigned attributes such as encoding information and display attributes.
A user MAY specify non-standardized user-defined attributes.
The notions "definition" and "declaration" of variables, constants, types and other language elements ARE used interchangeably and have equal meaning on the level of TTCN-3.
A TTCN-3 identifier IS case sensitive.
A TTCN-3 keyword SHALL be written in all lowercase letters.
A TTCN-3 keyword SHALL NOT be used as identifier of a TTCN-3 object.
A TTCN-3 keyword SHALL NOT be used as identifier of an object imported from a module of another language.
The name of a predefined TTCN-3 function SHALL NOT be used as identifier of a TTCN-3 object.
The name of a predefined TTCN-3 function SHALL NOT be used as identifier of an object imported from a module of another language.
A special TTCN-3 modifier IS an identifier prefixed with the @-symbol.
A modifier modifies the default semantics of the language element it is applied to in the specified way.
If more than one modifier is applied to a language element, the modifiers MAY be applied in any order.
A modifier CANNOT lead to backward incompatibilities with existing reserved keywords or identifiers.
A TTCN-3 module definition IS introduced by the keyword `module`.
A TTCN-3 module definition SHALL NOT be specified inside module definitions, the module control function, functions, altsteps, test cases or a component type.
An import of definitions from another module (keyword `import`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
An import of definitions from another module (keyword `import`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A grouping of definitions (keyword `group`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A grouping of definitions (keyword `group`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A data type definition (keyword `type`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A data type definition (keyword `type`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A communication port type definition (keyword `port`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A communication port type definition (keyword `port`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A test component type definition (keyword `component`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A test component type definition (keyword `component`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A signature definition (keyword `signature`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A signature definition (keyword `signature`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
An external function definition (keyword `external`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
An external function definition (keyword `external`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A constant definition (keyword `const`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part, in the module control function, in functions, altsteps and test cases, and in a component type.

A data or signature template definition (keyword `template`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part, in the module control function, in functions, altsteps and test cases, and in a component type.
A function definition (keyword `function`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A function definition (keyword `function`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
An altstep definition (keyword `altstep`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
An altstep definition (keyword `altstep`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A test case definition (keyword `testcase`) MAY be specified in the module definitions part.
A test case definition (keyword `testcase`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
A value variable declaration (keyword `var`) MAY be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps and test cases, and in a component type.
A value variable declaration (keyword `var`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module definitions part.
A template variable declaration (keyword `var template`) MAY be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps and test cases, and in a component type.
A template variable declaration (keyword `var template`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module definitions part.
A timer declaration (keyword `timer`) MAY be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps and test cases, and in a component type.
A timer declaration (keyword `timer`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module definitions part.
The module definitions part IS a basic unit of scope.
A component type IS a basic unit of scope.
A function IS a basic unit of scope.
An altstep IS a basic unit of scope.
A test case IS a basic unit of scope.
A statement block IS a basic unit of scope.
A template IS a basic unit of scope.
A user-defined named type IS a basic unit of scope.
A port type IS a basic unit of scope.
A statement block MAY include declarations.
A statement block MAY occur as a stand-alone statement block, embedded in another statement block or within a compound statement (e.g. as body of a while loop).
A built-in TTCN-3 type (e.g. integer, charstring, anytype) IS NOT a scope unit.
Every named user-defined type IS a scope unit, independent of its kind.
A scope unit consists of optional declarations.
A function (including the module control function), test case, altstep or statement block MAY additionally specify behaviour by using TTCN-3 program statements and operations.

A definition made in the module definitions part outside of other scope units IS globally visible and MAY be used elsewhere in the module, including all functions, test cases and altsteps defined within the module.
An identifier imported from another module IS globally visible throughout the importing module.
A definition made in a test component type MAY be used in a component type extending this component type.
A definition made in a test component type MAY be used in a function, test case or altstep that references that component type or a compatible test component type by a runs on clause.
Test cases, altsteps and functions ARE individual scope units without any hierarchical relation between them.
A declaration made inside the body of a test case, altstep or function SHALL only be used in that test case, altstep or function.
A declaration made in a test case IS NOT visible in a function called by the test case or in an altstep used by the test case.

A stand-alone statement block or a compound statement (e.g. if-else, while, do-while, `alt`) MAY be used within test cases, altsteps and functions, or embedded in other statement blocks or compound statements.
A statement block IS hierarchically related both to the scope unit including it and to any statement block embedded in it.
A declaration made within a statement block has local visibility.
A declaration of a scope unit at a higher hierarchical level IS visible in all units at lower levels within the same branch of the scope hierarchy.
A declaration of a scope unit at a lower hierarchical level IS NOT visible to units at a higher hierarchical level.

In the scope hierarchy, the module control function, component types, functions and altsteps without runs on clause, templates and user-defined named types ARE directly below the module definitions part.
In the scope hierarchy, a test case, and a function or altstep with runs on clause, IS below the component type referenced by its runs on clause.
In the scope hierarchy, statement blocks ARE below the module control function, functions, altsteps and test cases, and statement blocks MAY be nested.
The scope of a formal parameter of a parameterized object SHALL be restricted to the definition in which the formal parameter appears and to the lower levels of scope in the same scope hierarchy.
A formal parameter follows the scope rules for local definitions.
All identifiers in the same scope hierarchy SHALL be distinctive.
A declaration in a lower level of scope SHALL NOT re-use the identifier of a declaration in a higher level of scope in the same branch of the scope hierarchy.
The identifier of a module (its module name) or of an imported module belongs to the scope unit of the module.
The name of a module or of a module imported into it SHALL NOT be used as identifier for other definitions inside this module.
An identifier of a field of a structured type, of an enumerated value or of a group NEED NOT be globally unique.
Within the same module, the identifier of an enumerated value SHALL only be reused for enumerated values within other enumerated types or as identifier of a field of a structured type.
An enumerated value of an imported enumerated type SHALL NOT be used as the name of a value or template definition of that enumerated type.
The rules of identifier uniqueness SHALL apply to identifiers of formal parameters.
A declaration MAY be made in any order relative to other declarations, subject to the declaration-before-use rule for test case definitions, functions, altsteps and statement blocks.
A declaration inside a statement block MAY occur at any place where a statement can occur.
A declaration in the module definitions part MAY be made in any order.
A declaration in a component type definition MAY be made in any order.
A declaration inside a testcase definition, function, altstep or statement block SHALL be given before its first place of usage.
A local variable, local timer or local constant SHALL NOT be used before it is declared.
A label IS the only exception to the rule that declarations inside testcase definitions, functions, altsteps and statement blocks SHALL be given before their first place of usage.
A `goto` statement MAY reference a label that occurs later in the same statement block (forward reference).
A module MAY be parameterized.
A template MAY be parameterized.
A function MAY be parameterized.
An altstep MAY be parameterized.
A testcase MAY be parameterized.
An actual parameter MAY be a value, a template, a timer or a port.
Type parameterization IS NOT part of the TTCN-3 core language; it is defined in the optional package [i.12].
A module parameter SHALL be a value parameter (value parameterization only).
Module parameterization IS static parameterization that takes place at the start of runtime.
A module parameter SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type or the address type.
A template MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
Template parameterization IS dynamic parameterization that takes place at runtime.
A formal parameter of a template SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, or a template formal parameter.
A function MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
Function parameterization IS dynamic parameterization that takes place at runtime.
A formal parameter of a function SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type or the default type, or be a template or timer formal parameter.
An altstep MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
Altstep parameterization IS dynamic parameterization that takes place at runtime.
A formal parameter of an altstep SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type or the default type, or be a template or timer formal parameter.
A testcase MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
Testcase parameterization IS dynamic parameterization that takes place at runtime.

A formal parameter of a testcase SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type or a component type, or be a template formal parameter; port, default and timer formal parameters SHALL NOT be used.
A signature IS NOT a parameterizable object in the sense of table 2, because a signature only declares parameters.
A template for a signature CAN be parameterized.
A module, structured type, template, function, altstep or testcase MAY be defined incompletely, i.e. with entities (variables, templates, ports, timers, etc.) used in its definition left unresolved.
A module, structured type, template, function, altstep or testcase defined with unresolved entities IS called a parameterized object.
A formal entity replacing an unresolved entity in the definition of a parameterized object IS called a formal parameter.
A formal parameter of a parameterized template, function, altstep or testcase IS defined in a formal parameter list.
A formal parameter of a module IS defined in a module parameter definition.
A formal parameter SHALL be an in, inout or out parameter.
If not stated otherwise, a formal parameter IS an in parameter.
A formal parameter, whether in, inout or out, CAN be both read and set within the parameterized object.
A formal parameter MAY be used directly as an actual parameter of another parameterized object, e.g. in a function invocation or in a template instance.
If a parameter is passed by value (in and out parameters), the type compatibility rules of clause 6.3 SHALL apply between the actual parameter and the formal parameter.
If a parameter is passed by reference, strong typing SHALL be applied between the actual parameter and the formal parameter.
If a parameter is passed by reference, the actual parameter SHALL be of the same type as the formal parameter.
A formal in parameter MAY have a default value.
If no actual parameter is provided for a formal in parameter with a default value, the default value IS used as the value of the formal parameter.
An out formal parameter CAN be read within the parameterized object, but it does not inherit the value of its actual parameter.
An out formal parameter SHOULD be set before it is read within the parameterized object.
A formal value parameter or formal template parameter MAY be declared lazy using the `@lazy` modifier.
A lazy formal parameter IS evaluated as specified by the definition of lazy values or templates in clause 3.1.
A formal value parameter or formal template parameter MAY be declared fuzzy using the `@fuzzy` modifier.
A fuzzy formal parameter IS evaluated as specified by the definition of fuzzy values or templates in clause 3.1.
A formal value parameter or formal template parameter declared lazy or fuzzy MAY additionally be declared deterministic using the `@deterministic` modifier.
The value of a component variable used in the delayed evaluation of a lazy or fuzzy parameter CAN differ from its value at the time the parameterized function or altstep was called.
Assigning a default value to a lazy or fuzzy formal parameter does NOT change the semantics of the parameter.
When the default value of a lazy or fuzzy formal parameter is used as the actual value, it SHALL be evaluated in the same delayed way as if an actual parameter was provided.
A module SHALL support value parameterization only.
The parameterization of a module IS static at start of runtime.
A module parameter MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type or the address type.
A `template` definition MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
The parameterization of a `template` IS dynamic at runtime.
A formal parameter in the formal parameter list of a `template` MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type, the address type, or be a template parameter.
A `function` definition MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
The parameterization of a `function` IS dynamic at runtime.

A formal parameter in the formal parameter list of a `function` MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type, the default type or the timer type, or be a template parameter.
A `altstep` definition MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
The parameterization of a `altstep` IS dynamic at runtime.

A formal parameter in the formal parameter list of a `altstep` MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type, the default type or the timer type, or be a template parameter.
A `testcase` definition MAY have value parameterization and template parameterization.
The parameterization of a `testcase` IS dynamic at runtime.
A formal parameter in the formal parameter list of a `testcase` MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type, the address type or a component type, or be a template parameter.
A formal parameter of a `testcase` SHALL NOT be of a port type, the default type or the timer type.
A signature IS not listed in table 2 because a signature declares parameters only.
A template of a signature CAN be parameterized.
The lazy or fuzzy property of a formal parameter IS valid only in the scope where the name of the parameter is visible.
If a fuzzy formal parameter is passed as actual parameter to a formal parameter declared without a modifier, the parameter IS NOT fuzzy inside the called function.
If a fuzzy formal parameter is passed as actual parameter to a lazy formal parameter, the parameter IS lazy inside the called function.
A value of any basic type, any user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type, the timer type or the default type MAY be passed as a value parameter.

A formal value parameter has the syntax [ ( `in` | `inout` | `out` ) ] [ ( `@lazy` | `@fuzzy` ) [ `@deterministic` ] ] TypeOrNestedTypeDef ValueParIdentifier [ ArrayDef ] [ ":=" ( Expression | "-" ) ].
A formal value parameter CAN be used within the parameterized object in the same way as a value, e.g. in expressions.
A formal value parameter MAY be an in, inout or out parameter.
A formal value parameter without a parameterization keyword IS an in parameter.
The in parameterization of a formal value parameter MAY optionally be denoted by the keyword `in`.
An inout or out formal value parameter SHALL be specified by the keyword `inout` or `out` respectively.
A formal in value parameter MAY have a default value, given by an expression assigned to the parameter.
A formal value parameter of a modified template MAY inherit the default value of the corresponding parameter of its parent template.
Inheritance of a default value by a formal parameter of a modified template SHALL be denoted explicitly by the dash (don't change) symbol in place of the default value.
If a function is used for the initialization of a default value of an in parameter, side effects SHOULD be avoided during the evaluation of the default value.
A side effect during the evaluation of a default value CAN cause non-deterministic test executions.
A side effect during the evaluation of a default value CAN be avoided, e.g. by adhering to the rules of clause 16.1.4.
A module supports static value parameterization to support test suite parameters.
The value of a module parameter MAY be unresolvable at compile-time.
The value of a module parameter SHALL be resolved by the commencement of runtime.
At runtime, a module parameter value IS globally visible.
At runtime, a module parameter value SHALL NOT be changed.
A template, testcase, altstep or function supports dynamic value parameterization.
The dynamic value parameterization of a template, testcase, altstep or function SHALL be resolved at runtime.
A component reference or a default reference IS handled as a value parameter.
For a formal parameter receiving a component reference, the corresponding component type IS the type of the formal parameter.
For a formal parameter receiving a default reference, the type `default` IS the type of the formal parameter.
A `const`, `var`, `timer`, `control`, `record of`, `set of`, `enumerated`, `port`, `component` or subtype definition, a `group` or an `import` SHALL NOT be parameterized.
A formal value parameter of a template SHALL be an in parameter.
A formal value parameter of an altstep activated as a default SHALL be an in parameter.
A default value SHALL be provided only for a formal in parameter.
The expression of the default value of a formal parameter SHALL be compatible with the type of the parameter.
The expression of the default value of a formal parameter MAY be any expression that is well-defined at the beginning of the scope of the parameterized entity.
The expression of the default value of a formal parameter SHALL NOT refer to other parameters of the same parameter list.
The default value of a component type formal parameter SHALL be one of the special values `null`, `mtc`, `self` or `system`.
The default value of a port type, timer type or default type formal parameter SHALL be the special value `null`.
The dash (don't change) symbol SHALL be used only with formal parameters of modified templates.
A formal value parameter of a template SHALL comply with the restrictions specified in clause 15.0.
A formal value parameter declared `@lazy` or `@fuzzy` SHALL be an in parameter.
When a formal value parameter is referenced (e.g. in assignments, expressions or template bodies), the rules for variables SHALL apply.
Only a function or altstep definition SHALL have formal parameters of a port, timer or default type or of a type containing a direct or indirect element or field of a port, default or timer type.

A function or altstep started as test component behaviour SHALL NOT have formal parameters of a port, timer or default type or of a type containing a direct or indirect element or field of a port, default or timer type.
Only a function, altstep or testcase definition SHALL have formal parameters of a component type or of a type containing a direct or indirect element or field of a component type.

If a lazy or fuzzy formal value parameter is used in a deterministic context (during the evaluation of a snapshot or the initialization of global non-fuzzy templates), it SHALL be declared `@deterministic`.
A formal template parameter IS used to pass a template into a parameterized object.

A formal template parameter has the syntax [ `in` | `inout` | `out` ] TemplateModifier [ ( `@lazy` | `@fuzzy` ) [ `@deterministic` ] ] TypeOrNestedTypeDef ValueParIdentifier [ ArrayDef ] [ ":=" ( TemplateInstance | "-" ) ].
To accept templates or matching symbols as actual parameters, a formal parameter SHALL be declared with the keyword `template` before its type.
A formal parameter declared with the keyword `template` IS a template parameter.
A formal template parameter accepts as actual parameters the matching mechanisms of annex B appropriate for its type as well as the values of its type.
A formal template parameter CAN be used within the parameterized object in the same way as a template or a template variable.
A formal template parameter MAY be an in, inout or out parameter.
A formal template parameter without a parameterization keyword IS an in parameter.
A formal in template parameter MAY have a default template, given by a template instance assigned to the parameter.
A formal template parameter of a modified template MAY inherit the default template of the corresponding parameter of its parent template.
Inheritance of a default template by a formal template parameter of a modified template SHALL be denoted explicitly by the dash (don't change) symbol in place of the default template.
If a default template is used, it IS evaluated in the scope of the parameterized entity, not in the scope of the actual parameter list.
A formal template parameter MAY be restricted to accept only actual parameters containing a restricted set of matching mechanisms.
A restriction of a formal template parameter IS expressed by `omit`, `present` or `value`.
The restriction `template (omit)` MAY be replaced by the shorthand notation `omit`.
A formal template parameter of a template SHALL be an in parameter.
A formal template parameter of an altstep activated as a default SHALL be an in parameter.
A default template SHALL be provided only for a formal in template parameter.
The default template instance of a formal template parameter SHALL be compatible with the type of the parameter.
The default template instance of a formal template parameter MAY be any template expression that is well-defined at the beginning of the scope of the parameterized entity.
The default template instance of a formal template parameter SHALL NOT refer to other parameters in the same parameter list.
The default template of a component type formal template parameter SHALL be built from the special values `null`, `mtc`, `self` or `system`.
A formal template parameter SHALL comply with the restrictions specified in clause 15.0.
The dash (don't change) symbol SHALL be used only with formal template parameters of modified templates.
A formal template parameter declared `@lazy` or `@fuzzy` SHALL be an in parameter.
When a formal template parameter is referenced (e.g. in assignments, expressions or template bodies), the rules for template variables SHALL apply.

If a lazy or fuzzy formal template parameter is used in a deterministic context (during the evaluation of a snapshot or the initialization of global non-fuzzy templates), it SHALL be declared `@deterministic`.
A value, template, timer or port MAY be passed into a parameterized TTCN-3 object as an actual parameter.
An actual parameter list MAY be given in list notation, with the actual parameters in the same order as the formal parameters.
An actual parameter list MAY be given in assignment notation, explicitly using the names of the associated formal parameters.
An actual parameter list MAY be given in mixed notation, where the first actual parameters are given in list notation and the additional actual parameters in assignment notation.
An actual parameter has the syntax ( Expression | TemplateInstance | "-" ) | ParameterId ":=" ( Expression | TemplateInstance | TimerRef | Port ), where "-" skips a parameter.

An actual parameter passed by value to an in formal value parameter SHALL be a variable, a literal value, a module parameter, a constant, a value variable, an invocation of a value returning function or external function, a formal value parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope, or an expression composed of these.

An actual parameter passed to an out formal value parameter SHALL be a variable, a template variable, a formal value or template parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization), or a reference to an element of a variable, template variable or formal parameter of a structured type.
The dash symbol "-" MAY be used as an actual parameter for an out formal value parameter.
When the dash symbol "-" is used as an actual out parameter, a possible result for that parameter IS NOT passed back.

An actual parameter passed to an inout formal value parameter SHALL be a variable, a formal value parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization), or a reference to an element of a variable or formal value parameter of a structured type.
A reference to a string element CANNOT be passed by reference, because string types are not structured types.

An actual parameter passed to an in formal template parameter SHALL be a literal value, a module parameter, a constant, a variable, an invocation of a value or template returning function or external function, a formal value parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope, an expression composed of these, a template, a template variable, or a formal template parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope.

An actual parameter passed to an out formal template parameter SHALL be a template variable, a formal template parameter, or a reference to an element of a template variable or formal template parameter of a structured type.
The dash symbol "-" MAY be used as an actual parameter for an out formal template parameter.
When the dash symbol "-" is used as an actual parameter for an out formal template parameter, a possible result for that parameter IS NOT passed back.

An actual parameter passed to an inout formal template parameter SHALL be a template variable or formal template parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope, or a reference to an element of a template variable or formal template parameter of a structured type.
When an actual parameter passed to an in formal value or template parameter contains a value or template reference, the rules for using references on the right hand side of assignments SHALL apply.

When an actual parameter passed to an inout or out formal value or template parameter contains a value or template reference, the rules for using references on the left hand side of assignments SHALL apply.
The values of out formal parameters ARE passed back to the actual parameters in the order of the formal parameters in the definition of the parameterized TTCN-3 object.
The value of an out formal parameter IS passed back to the actual parameter only if a value is assigned to the out formal parameter within the invoked object.
If no value is assigned to an out formal parameter within the invoked object, the corresponding actual parameter remains unchanged when the invoked object completes.
An element of a structured value or template (record, set, record of, set of, union and anytype values or templates) MAY be passed by reference as an actual parameter.
Modification of a formal parameter to which an element of a structured value or template is passed by reference modifies the original structured value or template.

Before an element of a structured value or template is passed by reference, the rules for referencing the element on the left hand side of assignments ARE applied, expanding the structured value so that the referenced element becomes accessible.

Passing a part of a structured component variable as an actual inout parameter CAN have confusing effects, because changing either the inout formal parameter or the component variable can also change the other.
A part of a structured component variable SHOULD NOT be passed as an actual inout parameter to a function or altstep that accesses that component variable.
If a formal parameter is an out parameter or has been defined with a default value or template, an actual parameter NEED NOT be provided for that formal parameter.
If no actual parameter is provided for a formal parameter with a default value or template, the default value or template IS taken as the actual parameter.
The actual parameters of an actual parameter list ARE evaluated in the order of their appearance.
If no actual parameter is provided for an out formal parameter, the dash symbol "-" IS taken as the actual parameter.
If no actual parameter is provided for an in formal parameter, the default value of the in formal parameter IS taken as the actual parameter.
The default values of formal parameters ARE evaluated after the evaluation of the actual parameters.
The default values of formal parameters ARE evaluated in the order of their formal parameters in the formal parameter list.
If assignment notation is used for the actual parameter list, the order of evaluation of the actual parameters CAN differ from the order of the formal parameters in the formal parameter list.
The empty parentheses of an instance of a parameterized template whose formal parameters all have default values MAY be omitted when no actual parameters are provided.
When list notation is used, the order of the actual parameters in the actual parameter list SHALL be the same as the order of the formal parameters in the corresponding formal parameter list.
When list notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each inout formal parameter.
When list notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each in formal parameter without a default value.
The actual parameter for an out formal parameter or for an in formal parameter with a default value MAY be skipped by using the dash symbol "-" as actual parameter.

An actual parameter MAY be skipped by leaving it out if no other actual parameter follows in the actual parameter list, either because the formal parameter is the last one or because all following formal parameters are out parameters or have default values and are left out.
The number of actual parameters in list notation SHALL NOT exceed the number of formal parameters in the formal parameter list.
When assignment notation is used, each formal parameter SHALL be assigned an actual parameter at most once.
When assignment notation is used, a formal parameter with the same name SHALL exist for each assigned actual parameter.
When assignment notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each formal parameter without a default value.
When assignment notation is used and the default value of a formal parameter is to be used, an assignment for that formal parameter SHALL NOT be provided.
The type of an actual parameter for an in formal parameter SHALL be compatible with the type of the formal parameter.
The type of an out formal parameter SHALL be compatible with the type of the actual parameter.
The type of an actual parameter for an inout formal parameter SHALL fulfil strong typing with respect to the type of the formal parameter.
The template restriction of an actual parameter for an in formal template parameter SHALL NOT be less restrictive than the template restriction of the formal parameter.
The template restriction of an actual parameter for an out formal template parameter SHALL NOT be more restrictive than the template restriction of the formal parameter.
The template restriction of an actual parameter for an inout formal template parameter SHALL be the same as the template restriction of the formal parameter.
An actual parameter passed to a restricted formal template parameter SHALL obey the restrictions given in clause 15.8.
A parameterized entity specified as an actual parameter SHALL have its own actual parameters provided in the top-level actual parameter list.
If the formal parameter list of a function, testcase, altstep or external function is empty, empty parentheses SHALL be included in the declaration of that object.
If the formal parameter list of a function, testcase, altstep or external function is empty, empty parentheses SHALL be included in each invocation of that object.
Empty parentheses SHALL be omitted in the declaration and invocation of an object with an empty formal parameter list that is not a function, testcase, altstep or external function.
Unless specified differently in the relevant clause, an actual parameter passed to an in or inout formal parameter SHALL be at least partially initialized.
A function called by an actual parameter passed to a fuzzy or lazy formal parameter SHALL NOT have inout or out formal parameters.
A function called by an actual parameter passed to a fuzzy or lazy formal parameter MAY internally call other functions that have inout or out formal parameters.
An actual parameter passed to an out or inout formal parameter SHALL NOT be a reference to a lazy or fuzzy variable.

If a value or template of a record, set, union, record of, set of, array or anytype type is passed as an actual parameter to an inout formal parameter, no field or element of that structured value or template SHALL be passed as an actual parameter to another inout formal parameter of the same parameterized TTCN-3 object.

The prohibition on passing fields or elements of a structured value or template passed to an inout formal parameter to another inout formal parameter of the same object applies recursively to all sub-elements at any level of nesting.

If two or more actual parameters passed to inout formal parameters of the same parameterized TTCN-3 object contain references to distinct alternatives of the same union or anytype value, a TTCN-3 tool SHALL produce an error.
If mixed notation is used, list notation SHALL NOT be used for any actual parameter following the first actual parameter in assignment notation.
If mixed notation is used, an actual parameter given in assignment notation SHALL NOT assign a formal parameter that already has an actual parameter given in list notation.
An actual parameter passed to a @deterministic fuzzy or lazy formal parameter SHALL fulfil the restrictions imposed on the content of functions used in special places given in clause 16.1.4.
The final formal parameter of a template, function, external function, altstep or testcase MAY have an ellipsis suffix.
A final formal parameter with an ellipsis suffix IS called a variadic parameter.
A variadic parameter accepts zero or more values of the specified type.
Inside the parameterized scope, the type of a variadic formal parameter IS a record of the specified type.
When list notation is used, the actual parameter for a variadic formal parameter MAY be absent from the actual parameter list or skipped by using the dash symbol.
If the actual parameter for a variadic formal parameter is absent or skipped, the actual parameter IS equal to an empty record of value or template.
When list notation is used, 1 to N comma-separated values of the specified type MAY be given as the actual parameter for a variadic formal parameter.

If comma-separated values are given for a variadic formal parameter, the actual parameter IS equal to a record of value or template that contains all the comma-separated values in their order of appearance.
When list notation is used, a single actual parameter of a compatible record of the specified type followed by an ellipsis MAY be given for a variadic formal parameter.
If a record of actual parameter followed by an ellipsis is given for a variadic formal parameter, the actual parameter IS passed directly to the variadic formal parameter.
When assignment notation is used for a variadic parameter, the actual parameter SHALL be a value or template of a compatible record of the specified type without an ellipsis.
When assignment notation is used for a variadic parameter, the actual parameter IS passed directly to the variadic formal parameter.
A variadic formal parameter SHALL be an in parameter.
A variadic formal parameter SHALL NOT have inout or out parameterization.
A TTCN-3 tool SHALL produce an error if the ellipsis is used in the declaration of a formal parameter that is not the last in the formal parameter list.

A direct or indirect cyclic definition SHALL NOT be used, except for recursive type definitions, recursive function or altstep definitions, and cyclic imports that form only allowed cyclic definitions.
A type definition MAY be recursive (cyclic).
A function or altstep definition MAY be cyclic, i.e. functions and altsteps MAY be called recursively.
Import definitions MAY be cyclic if the imported definitions form only allowed cyclic definitions.
An indirect cyclic definition CAN result from imports of definitions that are needed for the usage of a definition but need not be known in the importing module.
Only the main identifiers of a definition ARE used for the detection of cyclic definitions.
Field identifiers ARE NOT used for the detection of cyclic definitions.
The TTCN-3 language IS providing a number of predefined basic types.
The basic types IS including integer, boolean and string types as well as TTCN-3 specific types such as `verdicttype`.
A structured type such as a record type, set type or union type CAN be constructed from basic types.
An enumerated type IS a specific structured type constructed of enumerated values.
The `anytype` IS the union of all known types and the address type defined within a TTCN-3 module.
In a value or template of type `anytype`, only the known types of the specific module context SHALL be accessible.
The special configuration types `address`, `port` and `component` MAY be used to define the architecture of the test system.
The special type `default` MAY be used for default handling.
The TTCN-3 language IS providing the simple basic types `integer`, `float`, `boolean` and `verdicttype`.
The `integer` type IS a type with distinguished values which are the positive and negative whole numbers, including zero.
An integer value SHALL be denoted by one or more digits.
The first digit of an integer value notation SHALL NOT be zero unless the value is 0.
The integer value zero SHALL be represented by a single zero.
The `float` type IS a type to describe floating-point numbers and special float values.

A floating-point number IS in general defined as <mantissa> × <base>^<exponent>, where the mantissa is a positive or negative integer, the base a positive integer and the exponent a positive or negative integer.
The TTCN-3 floating-point value notation IS restricted to the base 10.
A float value CAN be expressed in two forms of value notation: the decimal notation and the exponent notation.
The decimal float value notation IS a sequence of digits containing a dot, e.g. 1.23 (123 × 10^-2), 2.783 or -123.456789.
The `integer` type IS a simple basic type.
A `integer` type MAY be subtyped by range subtyping and list subtyping.
The `float` type IS a simple basic type.
A `float` type MAY be subtyped by range subtyping and list subtyping.
The `boolean` type IS a simple basic type.
A `boolean` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `verdicttype` type IS a simple basic type.
A `verdicttype` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `bitstring` type IS a basic string type.
A `bitstring` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping and length subtyping.
The `hexstring` type IS a basic string type.
A `hexstring` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping and length subtyping.
The `octetstring` type IS a basic string type.
A `octetstring` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping and length subtyping.
The `charstring` type IS a basic string type.
A `charstring` type MAY be subtyped by range, list, length and pattern subtyping.
The `universal charstring` type IS a basic string type.
A `universal charstring` type MAY be subtyped by range, list, length and pattern subtyping.
The `record` type IS a structured type.
A `record` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `record of` type IS a structured type.
A `record of` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping and length subtyping.
The `set` type IS a structured type.
A `set` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `set of` type IS a structured type.
A `set of` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping and length subtyping.
The `enumerated` type IS a structured type.
A `enumerated` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `union` type IS a structured type.
A `union` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `map` type IS a structured type.
A `map` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `anytype` type IS a special data type.
A `anytype` type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.
The `address` type IS a special configuration type.
The `address` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
The `port` type IS a special configuration type.
The `port` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
The `component` type IS a special configuration type.
The `component` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
The `default` type IS a special default type.
The `default` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
The array notation `[]` IS listed as a separate class of type in the TTCN-3 type overview.
An array type MAY be subtyped by list subtyping.

List subtyping of record, record of, set, set of, enumerated, union, map and array types MAY be applied only when defining a new constrained type from an already existing parent type, not directly at the declaration of the first parent type.
The exponent float value notation IS two numbers separated by `E`, where the first number specifies the mantissa and the second specifies the exponent, e.g. 12.3E4 or -12.3E-4.
The mantissa in the TTCN-3 float value notation MAY be a decimal number as well as an integer.
The special values of the `float` type IS `infinity` (positive infinity), `-infinity` (negative infinity) and `not_a_number`.
The value `-not_a_number` SHALL NOT be used.
The `boolean` type IS a type consisting of two distinguished values.
A boolean value SHALL be denoted by `true` or `false`.
The `verdicttype` IS a type for use with test verdicts consisting of 5 distinguished values.
A `verdicttype` value SHALL be denoted by `pass`, `fail`, `inconc`, `none` or `error`.
The TTCN-3 language IS providing the basic string types `bitstring`, `hexstring`, `octetstring`, `charstring` and `universal charstring`.
The `bitstring` type IS a type whose distinguished values are the ordered sequences of zero, one, or more bits.
A `bitstring` value SHALL be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of the bit digits 0 and 1, preceded by a single quote (') and followed by the pair of characters 'B.
A `bitstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
A newline within a `bitstring` value notation SHALL be preceded by a backslash ("\").
Whitespaces, newline characters and backslashes within a `bitstring` value notation ARE ignored for the value and length calculation.
The `hexstring` type IS a type whose distinguished values are the ordered sequences of zero, one, or more hexadecimal digits, each corresponding to an ordered sequence of four bits.
A `hexstring` value SHALL be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of the hexadecimal digits 0-9, a-f, A-F, preceded by a single quote (') and followed by the pair of characters 'H.
Uppercase and lowercase letters MAY equally be used as hexadecimal digits in a `hexstring` value.
Each hexadecimal digit of a `hexstring` value IS denoting the value of a semi-octet using a hexadecimal representation.
A `hexstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
A newline within a `hexstring` value notation SHALL be preceded by a backslash ("\").
Whitespaces, newline characters and backslashes within a `hexstring` value notation ARE ignored for the value and length calculation.

The `octetstring` type IS a type whose distinguished values are the ordered sequences of zero or a positive even number of hexadecimal digits, every pair of digits corresponding to an ordered sequence of eight bits.
An `octetstring` value SHALL be denoted by hexadecimal digits 0-9, a-f, A-F, preceded by a single quote (') and followed by the pair of characters 'O.
The number of hexadecimal digits in an `octetstring` value notation SHALL be even (possibly zero).
Uppercase and lowercase letters MAY equally be used as hexadecimal digits in an `octetstring` value.
Each hexadecimal digit of an `octetstring` value IS denoting the value of a semi-octet using a hexadecimal representation.
A `octetstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
A newline within a `octetstring` value notation SHALL be preceded by a backslash ("\").
Whitespaces, newline characters and backslashes within a `octetstring` value notation ARE ignored for the value and length calculation.
The `charstring` type IS a type whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters of the version of Recommendation ITU-T T.50 complying with the International Reference Version (IRV).
The IRV version of Recommendation ITU-T T.50 IS equivalent to the IRV version of the International Reference Alphabet (former International Alphabet No.5 - IA5).
A `charstring` value SHALL be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of non-control characters from the ITU-T T.50 IRV character set, preceded and followed by a double quote (").
The graphical characters of the `charstring` character set ARE including the range from SP(32) to TILDE(126).
A `charstring` value MAY be calculated using the predefined conversion function `int2char` with the integer value of its encoding as argument.
The predefined conversion function `int2char` IS returning single-character-length values only.
A double quote character (") within a `charstring` value notation IS represented by a pair of double quotes on the same line with no intervening space characters.
The `universal charstring` type (the `charstring` type preceded by the keyword `universal`) IS a type whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters from ISO/IEC 10646.
A `universal charstring` value MAY be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of characters from ISO/IEC 10646, preceded and followed by a double quote (").
A `universal charstring` value MAY be calculated using the predefined conversion function `int2unichar` with the integer value of its encoding as argument.
A `universal charstring` value MAY be denoted by a quadruple.
A `universal charstring` value MAY be denoted using the USI-like notation.
When the double quote format is applied, all characters from any character set defined in ISO/IEC 10646 ARE allowed in a `universal charstring` value.
A TTCN-3 user SHOULD be aware of the character set capabilities of the editing tool and of the TTCN-3 module transfer syntax UTF-8.
The predefined conversion function `int2unichar` IS returning single-character-length values only.
A double quote character (") within a `universal charstring` value notation IS represented by a pair of double quotes on the same line with no intervening space characters.

A quadruple IS denoting a character by the decimal values of its group, plane, row and cell according to ISO/IEC 10646, written as the keyword `char` followed by the four values separated by commas and enclosed in parentheses.
A quadruple IS denoting exactly one single character.
The double quote notation and the quadruple notation MAY be mixed within a single notation for a `universal charstring` value by using the concatenation operator `&`.
The USI-like notation MAY be used to denote 1..N characters using their short identifiers of code point.
The USI-like notation IS composed of the keyword `char` followed by parentheses.
The parentheses of the USI-like notation ARE enclosing a comma-separated list of short identifiers.
Each short identifier in the USI-like notation IS representing a single character.
A short identifier SHALL be composed of a letter U or u, followed by an optional "+" PLUS SIGN character, followed by 1..8 hexadecimal digits.
The hexadecimal digits of a short identifier ARE representing the numeric code point of the character.
Leading zeroes of a short identifier in the USI-like notation MAY be omitted (char(U171) is equal to char(U0171)).
A control character CAN be denoted in a `universal charstring` value by the predefined conversion function, the quadruple form or the USI-like notation.
By default, a `universal charstring` SHALL conform to the UTF-32 encoding specified in clause 9.3 of ISO/IEC 10646.
UTF-32 IS an encoding format representing any UCS character on a fixed, 32 bits-length field.
The default UTF-32 encoding of a `universal charstring` MAY be overridden using the defined variant attributes.
The useful character string types `utf8string`, `bmpstring`, `utf16string` and `iso8859string` ARE defined in annex E using the variant attributes.
The general term string or string type IS referring to `bitstring`, `hexstring`, `octetstring`, `charstring` and `universal charstring`.
The general term binary string or binary string type IS referring to `bitstring`, `hexstring` and `octetstring`.
The general term character string or character string type IS referring to `charstring` and `universal charstring`.
An individual element of a string value MAY be accessed using the index notation (array-like syntax).
The index notation applied to a string value SHALL access only a single element of the string.
Assigning a string of length 0 or of length greater than 1 to a string element using the index notation SHALL cause an error.
The indexing of string elements SHALL begin with the value zero (0).
When retrieving an element from a string, the index SHALL be between zero and the length of the string minus one.
Retrieving an element from a string with an index outside the range zero to the length of the string minus one SHALL cause an error.
When assigning an element to the end of a string, the length of the string SHOULD be used as index.
Assigning an element to a string with an index larger than the length of the string SHALL cause an error.
An uninitialized string MAY be initialized with a single element by using the index value zero (0).
Assigning a single element to an uninitialized string with an index other than zero (0) SHALL cause an error.
A user-defined type SHALL be denoted by the keyword `type`.
A user-defined type MAY define a subtype (such as a list, range or length restriction) of a basic type, a structured type or the `anytype` according to table 3.
A value of a subtype SHALL fulfil the conditions specified by the constraint of the subtype.
A value of a subtype SHALL fulfil all constraints of all direct and indirect parent types of the subtype up to the core type.
A subtype definition MAY specify a list of distinguished templates as subtype constraint, as listed in table 3.
Each template in a template list constraint SHALL be an instance of the type being constrained.
The set of values matching at least one template of a template list constraint SHALL be a subset of the values defined by the type being constrained.
A subtype defined by a template list constraint restricts its allowed values to the values matching at least one of the templates in the list.
A template in a template list constraint SHALL only reference (directly or indirectly) other templates or constant expressions.
A constant expression used (directly or indirectly) in a template of a template list constraint SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10 for constant expressions used in type definitions.
A subtype definition MAY specify a list of subtypes as subtype constraint, as listed in table 3.
Each type in a type list constraint SHALL be a subtype of the root type of the type being defined.
A subtype defined by a type list constraint restricts its allowed values to the union of the values of the referenced subtypes.
A range constraint MAY be specified for the types `integer`, `charstring`, `universal charstring` and `float` and for types derived from them.
For `integer` and `float`, a subtype defined by a range constraint restricts its allowed values to the values in the range, including or excluding the lower boundary and/or the upper boundary.
For `integer` and `float` range constraints, each range boundary MAY be inclusive or exclusive.
The upper boundary of a range constraint SHALL be greater than or equal to the lower boundary.
In an integer range constraint, `-infinity` MAY be used instead of a lower boundary value and `infinity` instead of an upper boundary value to indicate that there is no lower or upper boundary.
`-infinity` SHALL NOT be used as the upper boundary of an integer range constraint.
`infinity` SHALL NOT be used as the lower boundary of an integer range constraint.
In a `float` range constraint, `-infinity` or `infinity` MAY be used as the boundaries.
A `float` range constraint with `-infinity` as lower boundary does not restrict the allowed numerical values downward and includes the special value `-infinity`.
A `float` range constraint whose lower and upper boundaries both denote `-infinity` includes no numerical values and only the special value `-infinity`.
A `float` range constraint with `infinity` as upper boundary does not restrict the allowed numerical values upward and includes the special value `infinity`.
A `float` range constraint whose lower and upper boundaries both denote `infinity` includes no numerical values and only the special value `infinity`.
A `float` range constraint with an exclusive boundary `!-infinity` or `!infinity` includes the respective unrestricted numerical float values but not the special value `-infinity` or `infinity`.
The special value `not_a_number` SHALL NOT be used in a `float` range constraint.
For `charstring` and `universal charstring` types, a range constraint restricts the allowed values of each separate character in the strings.
The boundaries of a character string range constraint SHALL evaluate to valid (non-empty) character positions according to the coded character set table(s) of the type.
An empty position of the coded character set table between the lower and the upper boundaries of a character string range constraint is not a valid value of the range.
A constant used in a constant expression defining a range boundary SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10.
A length restriction MAY be specified on a string type.
The unit of the length boundaries of a length restriction depends on the string type with which it is used, as specified in table 4.
A length boundary of a string length restriction SHALL be an inclusive boundary only.
A length boundary of a string length restriction SHALL evaluate to a non-negative `integer` value (or a value of a type derived from `integer`).
The keyword `infinity` MAY be used as the upper boundary of a length restriction to indicate that there is no upper limit for the length.
The upper boundary of a length restriction SHALL be greater than or equal to the lower boundary.
A character pattern as specified in clause B.1.5 MAY be used to constrain the permitted values of `charstring` and `universal charstring` types.
A pattern subtype constraint SHALL consist of the keyword `pattern` followed by a character pattern.
All values denoted by the character pattern of a pattern subtype constraint SHALL be a subset of the values of the type being subtyped.
A constant used in a constant expression defining a pattern subtype constraint SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10.
Pattern subtyping CAN be seen as a special form of list constraint whose members are generated by a mechanism rather than listed explicitly.
An `integer` or `float` subtype definition (or a subtype definition of a type derived from them) MAY mix list and range constraints.
A subtype definition MAY mix template list and type list constraints with each other and with range constraints.
Overlapping of different constraints in a subtype definition is not an error.
The unit of length of a length restriction on `bitstring` is bits.
The unit of length of a length restriction on `hexstring` is hexadecimal digits.
The unit of length of a length restriction on `octetstring` is octets.
The unit of length of a length restriction on a character string type (`charstring`, `universal charstring`) is characters.
A `charstring` or `universal charstring` subtype definition SHALL NOT mix pattern, template list, type list or range constraints.
A `bitstring`, `hexstring` or `octetstring` subtype definition MAY mix list constraints and a length restriction.
A `charstring` or `universal charstring` subtype definition MAY add a length restriction to a list, range or pattern constraint.
When mixed with other constraints, the length restriction SHALL be the last element of the subtype definition.
A length restriction mixed with list, range or pattern constraints yields a value set that is the intersection of the value sets of those constraints and of the length restriction.
The keyword `type` is used to specify structured types: record types, record of types, set types, set of types, enumerated types, union types and map types.
A value of a structured type MAY be given using assignment notation, value list notation or mixed list and assignment notation, as applicable to the type.
Assignment notation and mixed notation MAY be used for record, record of, set, set of and map values and for arrays.
In assignment notation or mixed notation, an assigned field or index SHALL NOT appear more than once.
In mixed notation, a field or index already given in the value list part SHALL NOT be assigned again in the assignment part.
Assignment notation MAY be used for union values.
Value list notation MAY be used for record, record of, set and set of values and for arrays.
Index notation MAY be used as the left-hand side of element assignments in assignment notation or mixed notation for record of, set of and map values and for arrays.
In index notation within an assignment or mixed notation, an index SHALL NOT appear more than once.
In index notation within an assignment or mixed notation, each index SHALL conform to the range of indices allowed by the type definition.
In mixed notation, an element in value list notation SHALL NOT follow an element in assignment notation within the same immediate context.
A TTCN-3 type definition MAY be recursive where applicable.
A recursive type definition SHALL be resolvable.
A recursive type definition SHALL NOT cause infinite recursion.
In a record or set type, a field referencing its own enclosing type SHALL be optional.
In a union type, at least one alternative SHALL NOT reference the union type itself.
A record type IS an ordered structured type.
A field of a record type MAY be of any TTCN-3 type.
Each field value of a record value SHALL be compatible with the type of the corresponding record field.
A field identifier of a record type IS local to that record type.
A field identifier SHALL be unique within its record type.
A field identifier of a record type NEED NOT be globally unique.
A record type MAY be defined with no fields (empty record).
A record value IS assigned on an individual field basis.
In value list notation for a record value, the order of the field values SHALL be the same as the order of the fields in the record type definition.
When the assignment notation is used for a record value, each field to be changed SHALL be identified explicitly.
In assignment notation for a record value, an explicitly identified field MAY be associated with a value, the not used symbol "-" or the `omit` keyword.
In assignment notation, the `omit` keyword SHALL only be used for optional fields.
An optional field assigned `omit` in assignment notation IS not present in the resulting value.
A mandatory field that is not explicitly referred to in the assignment notation, or is explicitly unspecified using the not used symbol "-", SHALL remain unchanged.
When a partial value is specified using the assignment notation at initialization, only the fields to be assigned values SHALL be specified.
At initialization with the assignment notation, a field not mentioned in the notation IS implicitly left uninitialized.
When a previously initialized value is re-assigned using the assignment notation, a field skipped or given the not used symbol "-" IS left unchanged.
A field SHALL NOT appear more than once in an assignment notation, also when a partial value is specified.
An omitted optional field IS intentionally not present in the record or set value and IS considered initialized, unlike an uninitialized field.
An omitted optional field IS NOT an obstacle to the record or set value being completely initialized.

When the assignment notation is used in a scope where the optional attribute is implicitly or explicitly set to "explicit omit", optional and mandatory fields not directly referred to in the notation SHALL remain unchanged.
An optional field of a variable that is not assigned explicitly IS uninitialized.
The optional attribute SHALL NOT have any effect on variables.
When the assignment notation is used in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", optional fields not directly referred to in the notation SHALL implicitly be set to `omit`.
When the assignment notation is used in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", mandatory fields not directly referred to in the notation SHALL remain unchanged.
In value list notation for a record value, every field listed SHALL be specified with a value, the not used symbol "-" or the `omit` keyword.
In value list notation, the `omit` keyword SHALL only be used for optional fields.
An optional field given `omit` in value list notation IS not present in the resulting value.
In value list notation, the n-th list component (a value, "-" or `omit`) IS associated with the n-th field of the record type.
A value list notation SHALL NOT contain an empty assignment (two commas immediately following each other or separated only by white space).
In value list notation, a field to be left unchanged that is followed by fields assigned a value or template explicitly SHALL be skipped by using the not used symbol "-".

When value list notation is used in a scope where the optional attribute is implicitly or explicitly set to "explicit omit", the remaining fields at the end of the type definition missing from the notation ARE left unchanged.

When value list notation is used in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", an optional field to be omitted by the implicit mechanism that is followed by explicitly assigned fields SHALL be skipped by using the not used symbol "-".

When all remaining fields at the end of the type definition are optional and are to be omitted by the implicit omit mechanism, the not used symbol "-" MAY be used for some or all of them, or they MAY be left out of the value list notation.

When a record value is assigned from a referenced value in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the uninitialized optional fields of the referenced value SHALL be set to `omit` in the new value.
When a record value is assigned from a referenced value in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the mandatory fields SHALL remain unchanged.
A field assignment in a record value or template MAY be prefixed by the `@fuzzy` modifier.

The right hand side of a `@fuzzy` field assignment SHALL only be evaluated when used in a matching, receiving or sending operation, as a non-lazy or non-fuzzy operand of an expression, as a non-lazy or non-fuzzy actual parameter, or on the right hand side of an assignment to a non-lazy or non-fuzzy variable, template variable or template.
A field of a record SHALL be referenced by the dot notation TypeIdOrExpression.ElementId.

In a dot notation, TypeIdOrExpression SHALL resolve to the name of a structured type or to an expression of a structured type, such as a variable, formal parameter, module parameter, constant, template or function invocation.
In a dot notation, ElementId SHALL resolve to the name of a field of the structured type.
A field of a record type definition SHALL NOT reference itself in its type (e.g. `MyType.field2 field2`).
The type of a field of a record type or record subtype referenced by dot notation IS the set of values allowed by the constraints of the field declaration itself.
Subtype constraints applied to the record type itself ARE ignored when a field type is referenced by dot notation.
Referencing a subfield of an uninitialized or omitted record field or value on the right hand side of an assignment SHALL cause an error.

When a field of an uninitialized record value or field, or of an omitted field (also omitted at a higher level), is referenced on the left hand side of an assignment, the reference SHALL recursively be expanded up to and including the depth of the referenced subfield.
When a record value or field is expanded, the subfield referenced in the dot notation SHALL be set to present.
When a record value or field is expanded, all unreferenced mandatory subfields SHALL be left uninitialized.
When a record value or field is expanded in a scope where the optional attribute is "explicit omit", all unreferenced optional subfields SHALL be left uninitialized.
When a record value or field is expanded in a scope where the optional attribute is "implicit omit", all unreferenced optional subfields SHALL be set to `omit`.
Expansion of record of, set of and array values SHALL follow clause 6.2.7, expansion of union values SHALL follow clause 6.2.5.1, and expansion of set values SHALL follow clause 6.2.2.1.
At the end of the expansion, the value on the right hand side of the assignment SHALL be assigned to the referenced subfield.
An optional field of a record type SHALL be specified using the `optional` keyword.
An optional field SHALL be omitted using the `omit` keyword.
A type of a record field MAY be defined nested within the record type definition.
A nested type definition of a record field MAY define a new structured type (record, set, enumerated, set of, record of, union or map).
A nested type definition of a record field MAY specify subtype constraints.
A field defined with a type reference but no explicit field name IS an embedded field.
The unqualified type name of an embedded field IS its field name.
A field of an embedded field whose name has no conflicts with other field names IS a promoted field.
A promoted field IS referenced like an ordinary field of the record.
A promoted field SHALL NOT be used as a field name in an assignment notation.
A set type IS an unordered structured type.
The ordering of the fields of a set type IS NOT significant; otherwise set types and values follow the rules of record types.
A field identifier of a set type IS local to that set type.
A field identifier SHALL be unique within its set type.
A field identifier of a set type NEED NOT be globally unique.
When value list notation is used for a set value, the values ARE assigned to the fields in the sequential order of the fields in the set type definition.
A field of a set SHALL be referenced by the dot notation.
A field of a set type definition SHALL NOT reference itself.
The rules of clause 6.2.1.1 for referencing field types of record types SHALL apply to referencing field types of set types.
An optional field of a set type SHALL be specified using the `optional` keyword.
A type of a set field MAY be defined nested within the set type definition, as for record types.
Embedded fields in a set type definition follow the same rules as embedded fields in record types.
A TTCN-3 tool SHALL support the specification of record of types and set of types, whose elements are all of the same type.
A record of type IS a record whose elements are all of the same type.
A set of type IS a set whose elements are all of the same type.
A record of type and a set of type ARE denoted using the keyword `of`.
An element of a record of type or set of type IS NOT associated with an element identifier.
A record of type IS similar to an ordered array.
A set of type IS similar to an unordered collection.
When the assignment notation is used for a record of or set of value, the elements to be changed ARE identified explicitly.
In an assignment notation for a record of or set of value, either a value or the not used symbol "-" MAY be assigned to an explicitly identified element.
When the assignment notation is used for a record of or set of value, an element not referred to in the notation SHALL remain unchanged.
When a partial record of or set of value is specified using the assignment notation, only the elements to be assigned values SHALL be specified.
When a partial record of or set of value is specified using the assignment notation, an element not mentioned IS implicitly left uninitialized.
An element of a record of or set of value MAY be left explicitly unspecified in an assignment notation using the not used symbol "-".
When a previously initialized record of or set of value is re-assigned with an assignment notation, an element that is skipped or assigned the not used symbol "-" SHALL remain unchanged.
In a value list notation for a record of or set of value, every element position up to the last list member SHALL be specified either with a value or the not used symbol "-".
In a value list notation, the n-th list member IS assigned to the n-th element of the record of or set of value.
A value list notation SHALL NOT contain an empty assignment (two commas with nothing or only white space between them).
An element to be left out of a value list notation assignment SHALL be explicitly skipped in the list by the not used symbol "-".
An already initialized element of a record of or set of value that has no corresponding list member at the end of a value list notation IS made uninitialized by the assignment.
Assigning the empty value list notation "{}" to a record of or set of value with initialized elements makes the value empty.
The index notation MAY be used on both the right hand side and the left hand side of an assignment.
An index notation on the right hand side of an assignment refers to the value of the identified element of a record of or set of value.
When the index notation is used on the left hand side of an assignment, only the value of the identified single element SHALL be changed and the values of the other elements SHALL remain unchanged.
The index of the first element of a record of or set of value SHALL be zero.
The index value in an index notation SHALL NOT exceed the limitation placed by length subtyping of the record of or set of type.
If the element indicated by an index notation on the right hand side of an assignment is uninitialized, this SHALL cause a semantic or runtime error.
Referencing an element of an uninitialized or omitted record of or set of field or value on the right hand side of an assignment SHALL cause an error.
If an index notation on the left hand side of an assignment refers to a non-existent element, the value at the right hand side IS assigned to that element.
If an index notation on the left hand side of an assignment refers to a non-existent element, every element with a smaller index and without an assigned value IS created with an uninitialized value.
For nested record of or set of types, an array or record of integer restricted to a single size MAY be used as a short-hand notation for a nested index notation.

When an element of an uninitialized record of or set of value or field or of an omitted field is referenced on the left hand side of an assignment, the reference SHALL be recursively expanded up to and including the depth of the referenced element.
When expanding a record of or set of value or value field, the element referenced by the index notation SHALL be set to present.
When expanding a record of or set of value or value field, all elements with a smaller index than the referenced element SHALL be created with an uninitialized value.
Expansion of record, union and set values and intermediate fields SHALL follow item a) of clauses 6.2.1.1, 6.2.5.1 and 6.2.2.1 respectively.
At the end of the expansion, the value at the right hand side of the assignment SHALL be assigned to the referenced element.
A record of or set of value SHALL NOT contain uninitialized elements except in transient states while the value remains invisible.
Sending a record of or set of value with uninitialized elements SHALL cause an error.
An assignment notation and an index notation used to change elements of a record of or set of value have a similar effect.
An assignment notation CAN address multiple elements in one notation, while an index notation CAN address a single element only.
The index notation CAN be used to copy record of values element by element in a for loop.
Embedded record of and set of types result in a data structure similar to multidimensional arrays.
The element type of a record of or set of type definition MAY be specified by a nested type definition.
A nested type definition within a record of or set of type definition MAY define a new record, set, enumerated, set of or record of type.
A nested type definition within a record of or set of type definition MAY specify subtype constraints.
The inner type of a record of or set of type MAY be referenced by using the index notation with a dash.
The notation TypeId[-], where TypeId resolves to the name of a record of or set of type, references the inner type of TypeId.
If the type definition of a record of or set of type restricts its element type, the inner type reference yields a type which contains all values of the constrained element type.
A length restriction of the outer record of type IS NOT part of the inner type yielded by an inner type reference.
A TTCN-3 tool SHALL support enumerated types.
An enumerated type IS a type that takes only values from a distinct named set of values.
A distinct named value of an enumerated type IS called an enumerated value.
An enumerated value SHALL have an identifier.
A reference to an enumerated value SHALL only use the identifier of the enumerated value.
A reference to an enumerated value IS either in unqualified or in qualified form.
The unqualified form of an enumerated value reference consists only of the identifier of the enumerated value.
The qualified form of an enumerated value reference consists of the enumerated type reference, followed by a dot and the enumerated value identifier.
The identifiers of the enumerated values SHALL be unique within the enumerated type.
The identifier of an enumerated value NEED NOT be globally unique.
The identifier of an enumerated value IS visible in the context of its enumerated type only.
For any instantiation or value reference of an enumerated type, the enumerated type SHALL be implicitly or explicitly identified.
If an enumerated type is the type of an element or field of a structured type, the enumerated type IS implicitly referenced via the given element or field at value assignment and instantiation.
