The value extraction IS the application of the `.value` notation to a template instance, extracting the underlying value from a `charstring` pattern matching mechanism or from a template with the omit restriction.
The value extraction has the syntax TemplateInstance "." `value`.
Applying the value extraction to a pattern matching mechanism of the form `pattern` StringValue IS yielding the value StringValue.
If the pattern operand of the value extraction contains any matching attribute, the value extraction SHALL remove that attribute.
Applying the value extraction to a template that evaluates to Value `ifpresent` IS yielding the value Value.
Applying the value extraction to a template that contains a value IS yielding that value.
Applying the value extraction to a template that contains neither a pattern, nor a value template with an `ifpresent` matching attribute, nor a value SHALL result in an error.
A function, an altstep and a testcase ARE used to specify and structure test behaviour, define default behaviour and structure computation in a module.
A function IS used to express test behaviour, to organize test execution or to structure computation in a module.

A function definition has the syntax `function` [`@deterministic` | `@control`] (FunctionIdentifier | `control`) "(" [{(FormalValuePar | FormalTemplatePar) [","]}] ")" [`runs on` ComponentType] [`mtc` ComponentType] [`system` ComponentType] [`return` [TemplateModifier] TypeOrNestedTypeDef [ArrayDef]] StatementBlock.
A function definition MAY carry at most one of the modifiers `@deterministic` and `@control`.
The `runs on`, `mtc`, `system` and `return` clauses of a function definition are optional and, when present, appear in this order before the statement block.
A function IS a portion of TTCN-3 behaviour that performs a specific task and is relatively independent of the remaining behaviour.
A function MAY return a value or a template.
A value return IS denoted in the function header by the `return` keyword followed by a type expression.
A template return IS denoted in the function header by the `return` keyword followed by a TemplateModifier and a type expression.
Execution of a return statement in the body of a function evaluates the return value or template.
Execution of a return statement in the body of a function terminates the function.
Execution of a return statement in the body of a function returns the result to the location of the call of the function.
The behaviour of a function CAN be defined by using the statements and operations described in clauses 18 to 26.
A function MAY be parameterized.
A function MAY have an mtc clause.
If a function has an mtc clause, the component type referenced by the mtc clause SHALL be mtc-compatible with the type of the mtc component reference.
If a function has no mtc clause, the type of the mtc component reference IS unknown in the scope of the function.
A function MAY have a system clause.
If a function has a system clause, the component type referenced by the system clause SHALL be system-compatible with the type of the system component reference.
If a function has no system clause, the type of the system component reference IS unknown in the scope of the function.
A function MAY be declared deterministic by using the `@deterministic` modifier.
A deterministic function IS safe to be called from specific places where non-determinism could lead to unexpected side effects.
The determinism of a function marked `@deterministic` IS NOT required to be exhaustively checked by a tool, as the determination of determinism is semi-decidable.
The `@deterministic` annotation IS mainly used for informational purposes and for allowing certain functions to be used during snapshot evaluation.
A function CAN be seen as deterministic if it does not violate any of the restrictions of clause 16.1.4; a violation of these restrictions does not automatically imply non-determinism.
A function without a `runs on` clause SHALL NOT locally invoke a function that has a `runs on` clause.
A function without a `runs on` clause SHALL NOT locally invoke an altstep that has a `runs on` clause.
A function without a `runs on` clause SHALL NOT activate as default an altstep that has a `runs on` clause.
A function started by the start test component operation SHALL have a `runs on` clause.
A function started by the start test component operation IS considered to be invoked in the component to be started, not locally.
The start test component operation MAY be invoked within behaviour without a `runs on` clause.
The restrictions concerning the `runs on` clause in clause 16.1.0 apply only to functions and altsteps and not to testcases.
A function called directly or indirectly from a module control function SHALL NOT have an mtc clause or a system clause.
A function called directly or indirectly from the module control function MAY execute testcases.
The formal parameter list of a function SHALL follow the rules for formal parameter lists defined in clause 5.4.
A return clause with a TemplateModifier SHALL obey the restrictions specified in clause 15.0.
A template return clause MAY be restricted to the matching mechanisms specific value and `omit` by a template restriction.
A return statement in a value returning function SHALL have a value expression compatible with the type specified in the return clause of the function header.

A return statement in a template returning function SHALL have a template reference (including a call of a value or template returning function) or a template instance compatible with the type specified in the return clause of the function header.
If the return clause of a template returning function has a template restriction, the returned template SHALL adhere to that template restriction.
If the function header includes a return clause, the function SHALL terminate by executing a return statement.
If a function with a return clause reaches the end of its function body without executing a return statement, a test case error IS caused.
If a function references names of definitions defined inside a component type definition, the function header SHALL reference that component type in a `runs on` clause.
A function MAY omit the `runs on` clause if all the necessary component-wide information is passed to the function as parameters.
An explicit control function SHALL obey the additional restrictions of clause 16.1.5.
Table 15 lists the statements and operations that a control function is allowed to use.
Invoking a function with mtc and system clauses from a function lacking a mtc or system clause CAN cause a runtime error.
A function with mtc and system clauses MAY invoke a function without mtc and system clauses.
A function IS invoked by referring to its name and providing the list of actual parameters.
A function invocation has the syntax FunctionRef "(" [{ActualPar [","]}] ")".
A function invocation results in the execution of the statement block of the invoked function.
The invoked function IS performed by the test component invoking it.
The actual parameters of a function invocation ARE passed into the statement block of the invoked function.
When the invoked function returns, the invoking test component continues its behaviour right after the function invocation.
A function that does not return a value SHALL be invoked directly (as a stand-alone statement).
A function that returns a value MAY be invoked directly or inside an expression.
The actual parameter list of a function invocation SHALL follow the rules for actual parameter lists defined in clause 5.4.
A function bound to a test component by the start test component operation SHALL obey the special restrictions described in clause 21.3.2.
When a function is invoked, the test component type of the invoking test component SHALL be compatible with the `runs on` clause of the invoked function as described in clause 6.3.2.7.

When a function is invoked, the mtc and system clauses of the invoked function SHALL be mtc- and system-compatible with the actual mtc and system types of the running test case as described in clause 6.3.2.7.
A function that returns an uninitialized value MAY be invoked only directly as a statement of a statement block or as the return value of a return statement.

Invoking a function that returns an uninitialized value in any other place than as a statement or as the value of a return statement (e.g. in an expression, as an actual parameter or on the right hand side of an assignment) SHALL cause an error.
The TTCN-3 language IS provided with a number of predefined (built-in) functions.
A predefined function NEED NOT be declared before use.
The predefined function `int2char` IS a conversion function that converts an integer value to a charstring value.
The predefined function `int2unichar` IS a conversion function that converts an integer value to a universal charstring value.
The predefined function `int2bit` IS a conversion function that converts an integer value to a bitstring value.

A predefined function invocation IS written as the function keyword followed by a parenthesized, comma-separated actual parameter list whose number and kind (SingleExpression or TemplateInstance, mandatory or optional) is fixed per function as given in the syntactical structure of clause 16.1.2 (e.g. int2bit(SingleExpression, SingleExpression), lengthof(TemplateInstance), substr(TemplateInstance, SingleExpression, SingleExpression), rnd([SingleExpression]), testcasename()).
The `regexp` predefined function invocation MAY carry the optional `@nocase` modifier between the keyword and the parameter list.

The actual parameters of `lengthof`, `sizeof`, `istemplatekind`, the first two parameters of `regexp`, the first parameter of `substr` and the first parameter of `encvalue`, `encvalue_unichar` and `encvalue_o` ARE TemplateInstances, while all other predefined function parameters ARE SingleExpressions.
When a predefined function is invoked, the number of actual parameters SHALL be the same as the number of formal parameters.
When a predefined function is invoked, each actual parameter SHALL evaluate to an element of the type of its corresponding formal parameter.

When a predefined function is invoked, every actual in and inout parameter SHALL be completely initialized, except as permitted for `lengthof`, `substr`, `replace`, `any2unistr`, `decvalue` and `decvalue_unichar`.
Any actual parameter of the predefined functions `lengthof`, `substr` and `replace` MAY be partially initialized.
The actual parameter for the `invalue` formal parameter of the `any2unistr` predefined function MAY be uninitialized or partially initialized.
The actual parameter for the `encoded_value` formal parameter of the `decvalue` and `decvalue_unichar` predefined functions MAY be uninitialized.
A function MAY be defined within a module or be declared as an external function (`external`).

An external function declaration has the syntax `external function` [`@deterministic` | `@control`] ExtFunctionIdentifier "(" [{(FormalValuePar | FormalTemplatePar) [","]}] ")" [`return` [TemplateModifier] Type].
The formal parameter list of an external function SHALL contain only value and template formal parameters (no timer or port formal parameters).
An external function declaration SHALL NOT contain a `runs on`, `mtc` or `system` clause.
An external function declaration SHALL NOT carry both the `@deterministic` and the `@control` modifier.
An external function declaration in a TTCN-3 module SHALL provide only the function interface (no statement block).
The realization of an external function IS outside the scope of the TTCN-3 core language standard.
An external function MAY be declared deterministic by using the `@deterministic` modifier.
A deterministic external function IS safe to be called from the specific places listed in clause 16.1.4, where non-determinism could lead to unexpected side effects.
The `@control` modifier of an external function IS used in the same way as for functions, as described in clause 16.1.5.
An external function SHOULD exchange information with the test system only via return values and parameter passing.
An external function SHOULD NOT cause side effects that change the status of the test system and may influence the test outcome.
A side effect that changes the status of the test system CAN occur if an external function contains default handling, configuration, communication or timer operations.

If a value returning function is called in a receiving communication operation (in templates, template fields, in-line templates as actual parameters or when evaluating the port expression), in a timeout operation (when evaluating the timer expression), in a guard or event of an alt statement or altstep, or in the initialization of an altstep local definition, the function SHALL NOT contain any of the operations listed in clause 16.1.4 items a) to m).

The restriction on operations in functions called from snapshot-evaluation contexts IS intended to avoid side effects that change the component state or the actual snapshot and to prevent different results of subsequent evaluations on an unchanged snapshot.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain a component operation (`create`, `start` (component), `stop` (component), `kill`, `running` (component), `alive`, `done` or `killed`).

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain a port operation (`start` (port), `stop` (port), `halt`, `clear`, `checkstate`, `send`, `receive`, `trigger`, `call`, `getcall`, `reply`, `getreply`, `raise`, `catch`, `check`, `connect`, `disconnect`, `map` or `unmap`).

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain the `action` operation.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain a timer operation (`start` (timer), `stop` (timer), `running` (timer), `read` or `timeout`).

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT call a non-deterministic external function.

A non-deterministic external function IS an external function whose resulting values for actual inout or out parameters or whose return value may differ for different invocations with the same actual in and inout parameters.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT call the `rnd` predefined function.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT use a component variable on the left-hand side of an assignment.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT pass a component variable as actual parameter to an `out` or `inout` formal parameter.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT call the `setverdict` operation.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain the `activate` or `deactivate` statement.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain the `deactivate` statement.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT call a function or a deterministic external function with `out` or `inout` parameters.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT call a function or external function that has `@fuzzy` formal parameters or `@fuzzy` variables.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT contain the `setencode` operation.

A function called (directly or indirectly) in a receiving communication operation, a timeout operation, an alt statement or altstep guard or event, or an altstep local definition initialization SHALL NOT reference a lazy or fuzzy variable, parameter or template that has not been declared deterministic.
The execution of the operations `start`, `stop`, `done`, `killed`, `halt`, `clear`, `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply`, `catch` and `check` CAN cause changes to the current snapshot.
The use of the operations `send`, `call`, `reply`, `raise` and `action` in a function called from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because all communication is to be made explicit.

The use of the operations `map`, `unmap`, `connect`, `disconnect` and `create` in a function called from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because all configuration operations are to be made explicit.

Calling non-deterministic external functions, `rnd`, `running`, `alive`, `read`, `checkstate` or `setverdict`, referencing fuzzy objects and writing to component variables in a function called from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because it may lead to different results of subsequent evaluations of the same snapshot (e.g. rendering deadlock detection impossible).

The use of the `activate` and `deactivate` operations in a function called from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because they modify the set of defaults considered during the evaluation of the current snapshot.

The restrictions of clause 16.1.4, except restriction j) on out or inout parameterization, apply recursively, i.e. the restricted operations SHALL NOT be used directly or via an arbitrarily long chain of function invocations.

A function called from a snapshot-evaluation context MAY call functions that themselves call functions or deterministic external functions with out or inout parameters, because restriction j) does not apply recursively.

Using out or inout parameters or the `setencode` operation in a function called from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because it may lead to different results of subsequent evaluations of the same snapshot.

Calling functions and external functions with `@fuzzy` parameters from a snapshot-evaluation context IS an error, because fuzzy objects are re-evaluated each time they are referenced, which may lead to different results of subsequent evaluations of the same snapshot.
An explicit control function IS declared either by use of the name `control` or by use of the `@control` modifier.

An altstep IS used to specify default behaviour or to structure the alternatives of an `alt` statement.

An altstep definition has the syntax `altstep` [`@control`] [`interleave`] AltstepIdentifier "(" [{(FormalValuePar | FormalTemplatePar) [","]}] ")" [`runs on` ComponentType] [`mtc` ComponentType] [`system` ComponentType] "{" {(VarInstance | TimerInstance | ConstDef | TemplateDef) [";"]} AltGuardList "}".
An altstep IS a scope unit similar to a function.
An altstep body IS composed of an optional set of local definitions and a set of alternatives.
An alternative of an altstep body IS called a top alternative.
The syntax rules of the top alternatives of an altstep ARE identical to the syntax rules of the alternatives of an `alt` statement.
An altstep MAY define a named interleave statement by usage of the `interleave` keyword.
If an altstep is defined with the `interleave` keyword, the syntax rules of its top alternatives ARE identical to the syntax rules of the alternatives of an `interleave` statement.
The usage of an interleave altstep IS NOT subject to further restrictions than the usage of a normal altstep, because an interleave statement is semantically equivalent to the expanded alt statement.
An interleave altstep and a normal altstep CAN both be used as activated default alternatives and as top-level alternatives in other `alt` statement blocks.
The behaviour of an altstep CAN be defined by using the program statements and operations summarized in clause 18.
An altstep CAN invoke functions and altsteps.
An altstep CAN activate altsteps as defaults.
An altstep MAY be parameterized as defined in clause 5.4.
An altstep MAY have an `mtc` clause.
If an altstep has an `mtc` clause, the component type referenced by the `mtc` clause SHALL be mtc-compatible with the type of the mtc component reference.
If an altstep has no `mtc` clause, the type of the mtc component reference IS unknown in the scope of the altstep.
An altstep MAY have a `system` clause.
If an altstep has a `system` clause, the component type referenced by the `system` clause SHALL be system-compatible with the type of the system component reference.
If an altstep has no `system` clause, the type of the system component reference IS unknown in the scope of the altstep.
An altstep with the `@control` modifier SHALL be executed only on the control component.
An altstep with the `@control` modifier SHALL fulfil the restrictions specified for functions with the `@control` modifier.
A local definition of an altstep SHALL be defined before the set of top alternatives.
The evaluation of default values of formal parameters and the initialization of local definitions of an altstep by calling value returning functions CAN have side effects.
The default value of a formal parameter of an altstep SHALL fulfil the restrictions given in clause 16.1.4.
The initialization of a local definition of an altstep SHALL fulfil the restrictions given in clause 16.1.4.
If an altstep includes port operations or uses component variables, component constants or component timers, the altstep header SHALL reference the associated component type by a `runs on` clause.
If all ports, variables, constants and timers used within an altstep are passed in as parameters, the altstep MAY omit the `runs on` clause.
An altstep without a `runs on` clause SHALL NOT locally invoke a function or altstep with a `runs on` clause.
An altstep without a `runs on` clause SHALL NOT locally activate an altstep with a `runs on` clause as default.
An altstep that is activated as a default SHALL only have `in` value or `in` template parameters.
An altstep that is only invoked as an alternative in an `alt` statement or as a stand-alone statement MAY have `in`, `out` and `inout` parameters.
The formal parameter list of an altstep SHALL follow the rules for formal parameter lists defined in clause 5.4.
An altstep started by the start test component operation SHALL have a `runs on` clause.
An altstep started by the start test component operation IS considered to be invoked in the component to be started, not locally.
The start test component operation MAY be invoked within behaviour without a `runs on` clause.
If an altstep is an interleave altstep, all restrictions of the `interleave` statement SHALL apply to the top alternatives of the altstep.
An altstep invocation IS always related to an `alt` statement.
An altstep CAN be invoked either implicitly by the default mechanism or explicitly by a direct call within an `alt` statement.
An altstep invocation has the syntax [`@nodefault`] AltstepRef "(" [{ActualPar [","]}] ")".
An altstep invocation IS NOT causing a new snapshot to be taken.
The top alternatives of an invoked altstep ARE evaluated by using the actual snapshot of the `alt` statement from which the altstep was called.
If a new `alt` statement is specified and entered within a selected top alternative of an altstep, a new snapshot IS taken.
For an implicit invocation by means of the default mechanism, an altstep SHALL be activated as a default by an `activate` statement before the place of the invocation is reached.
An explicit call of an altstep within an `alt` statement IS written like a function invocation as an alternative.
When an altstep is called explicitly within an `alt` statement, the next alternative to be checked IS the first top alternative of the altstep.

The top alternatives of an explicitly called altstep ARE checked and executed in the same way as the alternatives of an `alt` statement, except that no new snapshot is taken when entering the altstep.

If all top alternatives of an explicitly called altstep have been checked without a matching branch and the call is not the last alternative of the `alt` statement, the next alternative of the `alt` statement IS evaluated.
If all top alternatives of an explicitly called altstep have been checked without a matching branch and the call is the last alternative of the `alt` statement, the default mechanism IS invoked.
If the selected top alternative of an explicitly called altstep ends with a `stop` statement, the test component IS terminated.
If the selected top alternative of an explicitly called altstep ends with a `repeat` statement, a new snapshot IS taken and the calling `alt` statement IS re-evaluated.

If the selected top alternative of an explicitly called altstep ends with a `break` statement or without an explicit `repeat` or `stop`, execution IS continued immediately after the calling `alt` statement.
An alternative in an explicitly invoked altstep CAN refer to a disconnected or unmapped port at the time of its evaluation.
A port IS owned by the receiving component.
Matching IS related to the top elements in the port queues.
A dynamically unmapped or disconnected port contributes to a snapshot in the same manner as a mapped or connected port.
An explicitly invoked altstep CAN execute receiving operations that empty the queues of unmapped and disconnected ports without causing a test case error.
An altstep MAY be called as a stand-alone statement in a TTCN-3 behaviour description.
A stand-alone call of an altstep IS a shorthand for an `alt` statement with only one alternative describing the explicit call of the altstep.
If the `@nodefault` modifier is placed before a stand-alone altstep call, the implicit `alt` statement IS also modified by `@nodefault`.

When an altstep is invoked, the component type of the `mtc` clause of the invoked altstep SHALL be mtc-compatible with the actual mtc type of the running test case.
When an altstep is invoked, the component type of the `system` clause of the invoked altstep SHALL be system-compatible with the actual system type of the running test case.

Unless specified differently in the relevant clause, every value and template used in a basic program statement SHALL be completely initialized.

The complete-initialization restriction on basic program statements IS applied to the components of the statement (e.g. the boolean condition of an `if` statement) and IS NOT applied to the content of statement blocks embedded in the statement.
A value MAY be assigned to a variable and a template MAY be assigned to a template variable.
An assignment IS denoted by the symbol `:=`.
An assignment has the syntax ValueRef `:=` followed by either an Expression or a TemplateBody.
During execution of an assignment, the right hand side of the assignment SHALL evaluate to a value or template that is at least partially initialized.
The effect of an assignment IS to bind the variable on the left hand side to the value of the expression or to a template.
An assignment uses the rules of passing by value.
If the assigned variable is of a type whose values are object references, only the reference IS copied by the assignment and the referenced object (e.g. component, timer or port) IS NOT copied.
If the assigned variable is not of an object reference type, the content being assigned SHALL be a copy of the evaluated right hand side.
An assignment IS processed from left to right, i.e. expressions in the left hand side are evaluated before those in the right hand side.
The evaluation of an assignment SHALL obey the operator precedence defined in table 6.

Unless the assignment is to a lazy or fuzzy variable or parameter, the right hand side IS evaluated completely before the resulting value or template is bound to the evaluated left hand side of the assignment.
When assignments are used within the right hand side of an assignment (due to assignment notation), the assignment evaluation rules apply recursively.
A structured value on the right hand side of an assignment SHALL be assigned completely to the variable on the left hand side of the assignment.
If a partially initialized value is assigned to a completely initialized variable, the fields uninitialized at the right hand side SHALL also become uninitialized at the left hand side.

When a direct or indirect element or field of a lazy or fuzzy variable is assigned, the variable SHALL be evaluated as much as necessary before the assignment, i.e. an ancestor of that element or field initialized with a function call SHALL be evaluated.
If a lazy or fuzzy variable is fully assigned, the variable NEED NOT be evaluated before the assignment.
An assignment IS denoted by the symbol `:=`.
The if-else statement IS denoted by the keywords `if (…) {…} else {…}`.
The select case statement IS denoted by `select case (…) { case (…) {…} case else {…}}`.
The for loop IS denoted by `for (…) {…}`.
The while loop IS denoted by `while (…) {…}`.
The do while loop IS denoted by `do {…} while (…)`.
The label and goto statement pair IS denoted by the keyword pair `label` / `goto`.
The stop execution statement IS denoted by the keyword `stop`.
The returning control statement IS denoted by the keyword `return`.
The statement for leaving a loop, alt, altstep or interleave IS denoted by the keyword `break`.
The statement for the next iteration of a loop IS denoted by the keyword `continue`.
The logging statement IS denoted by the keyword `log`.

If a sub-field or sub-element of a fuzzy variable is assigned that has an ancestor formerly assigned a function call, the function call IS evaluated once before the assignment and replaced by its result inside the variable.
After such an assignment, the other sub-fields and sub-elements of that ancestor, apart from the field or element being assigned, become non-fuzzy.
The right hand side of an assignment SHALL evaluate to a value, template, port or timer which is type compatible with the variable at the left hand side of the assignment.

When the right hand side of an assignment evaluates to a template (global or local template, in-line template, template variable or matching mechanism), the left hand side of the assignment SHALL be a template variable.
The right hand side of an assignment SHALL evaluate to an object that is at least partially initialized.

If the left hand side of an assignment is a reference to a non-optional value object (a value definition, a mandatory field, a record/set of/array element, a union alternative or a value parameter), the right hand side SHALL NOT be a reference to an omitted field or the `omit` symbol.
Using a reference to an omitted field in the right hand side of an assignment has the same effect as using the `omit` keyword.
A shorthand assignment MAY be used for an integer variable that is incremented by 1 or decremented by 1.
The statement `v_integer++` IS a shorthand form of `v_integer := v_integer + 1`.
The statement `v_integer--` IS a shorthand form of `v_integer := v_integer - 1`.
The if-else statement, also known as the conditional statement, IS used to denote branching in the control flow.

The if-else statement has the syntax `if (` [ (VarInstance | Assignment) `;` ] BooleanExpression `)` StatementBlock, followed by zero or more `else if (` [ (VarInstance | Assignment) `;` ] BooleanExpression `)` StatementBlock, optionally followed by `else` StatementBlock.
The notation `else if (BooleanExpression) StatementBlock [else StatementBlock]` IS a shorthand notation for `else { if (BooleanExpression) StatementBlock [else StatementBlock] }`.

The notation `if ((VarInstance | Assignment); BooleanExpression) StatementBlock [else StatementBlock]` IS a shorthand notation for `{ (VarInstance | Assignment); if (BooleanExpression) StatementBlock [else StatementBlock] }`.
The branching of the control flow of an if-else statement IS decided upon the value of the boolean expressions (the conditions).
Exactly one statement block of an if-else statement IS executed, namely the first one (in textual order) whose condition evaluates to true.
The statement block of the optional `else` branch IS executed if all preceding `if` and `else if` conditions are false.
A boolean expression of an if-else statement MAY be preceded by an init statement (variable declaration or assignment).
An init statement of an if-else statement IS executed before the boolean expression it precedes is evaluated.
The scope of a variable declared within an init statement SHALL be limited to the if-else statement, including its else branches.
The select case statement IS an alternative syntactic form of the if-else statement.

The select case statement has the syntax `select` "(" [(VarInstance | Assignment) ";"] SingleExpression ")" "{" followed by one or more list branches `case` "(" {TemplateInstance [","]} ")" StatementBlock, an optional else branch `case else` StatementBlock, and a closing "}".
The select case statement IS an alternative to nested if-else statements when comparing a value to one or several other values.
A select case statement IS composed of a header part and one or more branches.
An execution of a select case statement SHALL NOT execute more than one of its branches.
The header part of a select case statement SHALL contain an expression.
The expression in the header part of a select case statement MAY be preceded by an init statement (variable declaration or assignment).
The init statement of a select case statement IS executed before the header expression is evaluated.
The scope of a variable declared within the init statement of a select case statement SHALL be limited to the select case statement.
A list branch of a select case statement IS the `case` keyword followed by a list of one or more template instances and a statement block.
The last branch of a select case statement MAY be an else branch consisting of the `case` keyword followed by the `else` keyword and a statement block.
An else branch SHALL only appear as the last branch of a select case statement.
Every template instance in a list branch of a select case statement SHALL be of a type compatible with the type of the header expression.
A list branch of a select case statement IS selected, and its statement block executed, only if at least one of its template instances matches the value of the header expression.
When the statement block of the selected branch has been executed without jumping out by a goto statement, execution SHALL continue with the statement following the select case statement.
The statement block of an else branch IS executed if no branch textually preceding the else branch has been selected.
The branches of a select case statement ARE evaluated in their textual order.

If none of the template instances matches the value of the header expression and the select case statement contains no else branch, execution continues after the select case statement without executing any branch.
A TTCN-3 tool CANNOT in general decide whether the template instances of a select case statement overlap.
The template instances used in the branches of a select case statement SHOULD NOT overlap.
When the template instances of a select case statement do not overlap, a TTCN-3 tool CAN provide better runtime performance.
The handling of non-overlapping template instances in a select case statement IS tool-specific.
When more than one branch of a select case statement could be selected because the template instances overlap, the textually first branch IS selected.
Overlapping template instances SHOULD NOT be used in the branches of a select case statement.
The handling of overlapping template instances in a select case statement IS tool-specific.
The SingleExpression in the header of a select case statement and every case template instance SHALL be type compatible.
If all template instances of all branches of a select case statement can be statically evaluated at compile time to specific values or value ranges, two branches SHALL NOT match the same value.
The select union statement IS a special form of the select statement for values of union types or anytype.

The select union statement has the syntax `select union` "(" [(VarInstance | Assignment) ";"] SingleExpression ")" "{" followed by one or more branches `case` "(" ({Identifier [","]} | {TypeIdentifier [","]}) ")" StatementBlock, an optional `case else` StatementBlock, and a closing "}".
A select union statement IS composed of a header part and one or more branches.
An execution of a select union statement SHALL NOT execute more than one of its branches.
The header part of a select union statement SHALL contain a template instance of a union type or of anytype.
The expression in the header of a select union statement MAY be preceded by an init statement (variable declaration or assignment).
The init statement of a select union statement IS executed before the header expression is evaluated.
The scope of a variable declared within the init statement of a select union statement SHALL be limited to the select union statement.

If the header template instance of a select union statement has a union type, each list branch SHALL start with the `case` keyword followed by one or more identifiers of alternatives (fields) of the union type.
If the header template instance of a select union statement has a union type, the last branch MAY be an else branch consisting of `case else` and a statement block.
If the header template instance of a select union statement has type anytype, each list branch SHALL start with the `case` keyword followed by one or more type names.
If the header template instance of a select union statement has type anytype, the last branch MAY be an else branch consisting of `case else` and a statement block.
The statement block of the list branch containing the identifier or type identifier of the chosen alternative IS executed.
If no case exists for the chosen alternative and an else branch is present, the statement block of the else branch IS executed.
If no case exists for the chosen alternative and no else branch is present, the select union statement HAS no effect.
The SingleExpression in the header of a select union statement SHALL be of a union type or anytype.
The SingleExpression in the header of a select union statement SHALL be at least partially initialized.
Every Identifier in a case of a select union statement SHALL be the identifier of an alternative of the union type of the header template instance.
Two cases of a select union statement SHALL NOT have the same case Identifier or TypeIdentifier.
The traditional form of the for statement IS a counter loop.
The counter loop for statement has the syntax `for` "(" (VarInstance | Assignment) ";" BooleanExpression ";" Assignment ")" StatementBlock.
A counter loop for statement IS composed of two assignments and a boolean expression.
The first assignment of a counter loop for statement SHALL initialize the index variable of the loop.
The boolean expression of a counter loop for statement IS the termination condition of the loop.
The second assignment of a counter loop for statement IS used to manipulate the index variable.
The value of the index variable of a counter loop IS increased, decreased or manipulated such that a termination criterion is reached after a certain number of iterations.
The termination criterion of a counter loop for statement SHALL be expressed by a boolean expression.
The termination criterion of a counter loop for statement IS checked at the beginning of each new loop iteration.
If the termination criterion of a counter loop for statement evaluates to true, execution continues with the statement block of the for statement.
If the termination criterion of a counter loop for statement evaluates to false, execution continues with the statement immediately following the for loop.
If a break statement is executed that is not within the body of an enclosed loop, alt statement, altstep or interleave statement, the for loop IS terminated.
The index variable of a counter loop MAY be declared before being used in the for statement.
The index variable of a counter loop MAY be declared and initialized in the for statement header.
If the index variable is declared and initialized in the for statement header, the scope of the index variable IS limited to the loop body.
The range-based loop IS a for statement that iterates over the elements provided by a range expression.
The range-based loop has the syntax `for` "(" [`var` TypeOrNestedTypeDef] ValueRef `in` Expression ")" StatementBlock.
The range expression of a range-based loop IS evaluated exactly once before the loop begins.
The range expression of a range-based loop MAY be partially initialized.
The range expression of a range-based loop SHALL evaluate to a value whose root type is record of, set of, array, octetstring, hexstring, bitstring, charstring or universal charstring.
A range-based loop iterates over the elements of the range expression in sequential order.
In each iteration of a range-based loop the corresponding element IS assigned to the iteration variable.
In each iteration of a range-based loop the statement block IS executed after the element has been assigned to the iteration variable.
If the iteration variable is declared in the for statement header, its scope and lifetime ARE limited to the statement block.
If the iteration variable is declared in the for statement header, a new iteration variable IS initialized in every iteration.
If the iteration variable is declared outside the for statement, its value after the execution of the loop IS that of the last iteration.
The assignment of an element to the iteration variable SHALL follow the assignment rules of clause 19.1.1.
An uninitialized element MAY be assigned to the iteration variable of a range-based loop.
When an uninitialized value is assigned to the iteration variable, the iteration variable IS uninitialized.
The iteration order of map keys and map values IS tool dependent and IS NOT guaranteed to be the same from one iteration to the next.
The behaviour of a lazy or fuzzy iteration variable IS NOT specified.
A lazy or fuzzy iteration variable SHOULD NOT be used, to avoid future compatibility issues.
A while statement IS a loop that is executed as long as the loop condition holds.
The while statement has the syntax `while` "(" [(VarInstance | Assignment) ";"] BooleanExpression ")" StatementBlock.
The loop condition of a while statement MAY be preceded by an init statement (variable declaration or assignment).
The init statement of a while statement IS executed before the loop condition is evaluated.
The scope of a variable declared within the init statement of a while statement SHALL be limited to the while statement.
The loop condition of a while statement SHALL be checked at the beginning of each new loop iteration.
If the loop condition of a while statement does not hold, the loop SHALL be exited and execution SHALL continue with the statement immediately following the while loop.
If a break statement is executed that is not within the body of an enclosed loop, alt statement, altstep or interleave statement, the while loop IS terminated.
A do-while statement IS a loop that is executed until the loop condition does not hold.
The do-while statement has the syntax `do` StatementBlock `while` "(" BooleanExpression ")".
A do-while loop IS identical to a while loop except for the point at which the loop condition is checked.
The loop condition of a do-while statement SHALL be checked at the end of each loop iteration.
The statement block of a do-while loop IS executed at least once before the loop condition is evaluated for the first time.
If a break statement is executed that is not within the body of an enclosed loop, alt statement, altstep or interleave statement, the do-while loop IS terminated.
A label statement MAY be used in test cases, functions and altsteps.
The label statement has the syntax `label` LabelIdentifier.
A label marks a statement.
A label IS used by the goto statement to transfer control to the labelled statement.
A label statement MAY be used like any other TTCN-3 behavioural program statement according to the syntax rules of annex A.
A label statement MAY be placed before or after a TTCN-3 statement.
A label statement SHALL NOT be the first statement of an alternative or top alternative in an alt statement, interleave statement or altstep.
A label defined by a label statement SHALL be unique among all labels defined in the same test case, function or altstep.
A goto statement performs a jump to a label.
The goto statement has the syntax `goto` LabelIdentifier.
A goto statement MAY be used in functions, test cases and altsteps to transfer control to a labelled statement.
A goto statement MAY jump forwards and backwards within a sequence of statements.
A goto statement MAY jump out of a single compound statement.
A goto statement MAY jump over several levels out of nested compound statements.
A goto statement SHALL NOT jump out of a function, test case or altstep.
A goto statement SHALL NOT jump into a function, test case or altstep.
A goto statement SHALL NOT jump into a sequence of statements defined in a compound statement (alt statement, while loop, for loop, if-else statement, do-while loop or interleave statement).
A goto statement SHALL NOT be used within an interleave statement.
The `stop` statement SHALL terminate the execution of a test component, a test case or the control behaviour.
The `stop` statement has the syntax `stop`.
The `stop` statement terminates execution in different ways depending on the context in which it is executed.
When executed in a control behaviour, the `stop` statement SHALL terminate the execution of the control component.
When invoked in a test case, altstep or function executed on a test component, the `stop` statement SHALL terminate that test component.
A `stop` statement that terminates a test component IS semantically identical to the stop component operation `self.stop`.
The `return` statement SHALL terminate the execution of a function or altstep.
The `return` statement has the syntax `return` optionally followed by an Expression or a TemplateInstance.
The `return` statement SHALL return control to the point from which the function or altstep was called.
A `return` statement used in a function MAY be associated with a return value or template.
An altstep call within an `alt` statement MAY be followed by an optional statement block.
If a statement block follows the altstep call in an `alt` statement, the `return` statement in the altstep SHALL return control to the beginning of that statement block.
If a statement block follows the altstep call in an `alt` statement and the altstep is left by a `return` statement, the statement block SHALL be executed before the `alt` statement is left.

If no statement block follows the altstep call in an `alt` statement, test execution SHALL continue with the first statement following the `alt` statement after the `return` statement in the altstep is executed.
The return value or template of a `return` statement SHALL be evaluated before control is returned.
A `return` statement SHALL NOT be present in a testcase definition.
The `log` statement provides the means to write logging information to some logging device.
A `log` statement MAY contain a module parameter identifier as a log item.
When a module parameter identifier is used in a `log` statement, the actual value of the module parameter IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a literal value as a log item.
When a literal value is used in a `log` statement, the value IS logged.
A literal value used as a log item in a `log` statement IS allowed to be free text.
A `log` statement MAY contain a data constant identifier as a log item.
When a data constant identifier is used in a `log` statement, the actual value of the constant IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a template instance as a log item.
When a template instance is used in a `log` statement, the actual template or field values and matching symbols IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a variable identifier as a log item.
When a variable identifier is used in a `log` statement, the actual value of the variable or "UNINITIALIZED" IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `self`, `mtc`, `system` or component type variable identifier as a log item.
When a `self`, `mtc`, `system` or component type variable identifier is used in a `log` statement, the actual value and, if assigned, the component instance name, otherwise "UNINITIALIZED" IS logged.
When a `self`, `mtc`, `system` or component type variable identifier is logged, the actual component state SHALL be logged as one of Inactive, Running, Stopped or Killed.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `create` operation as a log item.
When a `create` operation is used in a `log` statement, the actual state and the component instance name IS logged.
When a `create` operation is logged, the logged actual state IS always Inactive.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `running` operation (component or timer) as a log item.
When a `running` operation (component or timer) is used in a `log` statement, the return value (true or false) IS logged.
When a `running` operation on a component or timer array is logged, the array element specification SHALL be included.
A `log` statement MAY contain an `alive` operation (component) as a log item.
When an `alive` operation (component) is used in a `log` statement, the return value (true or false) IS logged.
When a `alive` operation on a component or timer array is logged, the array element specification SHALL be included.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `checkstate` operation as a log item.
When a `checkstate` operation is used in a `log` statement, the return value (true or false) IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a port instance as a log item.
When a port instance is used in a `log` statement, the actual state of the port IS logged.
When a port instance is logged, the port state SHALL be logged as Started or Stopped.
A `log` statement MAY contain a default type variable identifier as a log item.
When a default type variable identifier is used in a `log` statement, the actual state of the default or "UNINITIALIZED" IS logged.
When a default type variable identifier is logged, the default state SHALL be logged as Activated or Deactivated.
A `log` statement MAY contain an `activate` operation as a log item.
When an `activate` operation is used in a `log` statement, the activate operation (its actual state) IS logged.
When an `activate` operation is logged, the logged actual state IS always Activated.
A `log` statement MAY contain a timer name as a log item.
When a timer name is used in a `log` statement, the actual state of the timer IS logged.
When a timer is logged, the timer state SHALL be logged as Inactive, Running or Expired.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `read` operation as a log item.
When a `read` operation is used in a `log` statement, the return value IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `match` operation as a log item.
When a `match` operation is used in a `log` statement, the return value (true or false) IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `valueof` operation as a log item.
When a `valueof` operation is used in a `log` statement, the return value IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a `getverdict` operation as a log item.
When a `getverdict` operation is used in a `log` statement, the return value (none, pass, inconc or fail) IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a predefined function invocation as a log item.
When a predefined function invocation is used in a `log` statement, the return value IS logged.
A `log` statement MAY contain a function instance as a log item.
When a function instance is used in a `log` statement, the return value IS logged.
A function instance used as a log item in a `log` statement SHALL refer to a function with a return clause.
A `log` statement MAY contain an external function instance as a log item.
When an external function instance is used in a `log` statement, the return value IS logged.
An external function instance used as a log item in a `log` statement SHALL refer to an external function with a return clause.
The actual value or actual template logged by a `log` statement IS the value or template at the moment of the execution of the `log` statement.
The type of a value logged by a `log` statement IS tool dependent.
When an array identifier without array element specification is logged, the actual values of all array elements, and for component references the names of all array elements, SHALL be logged.
The string "UNINITIALIZED" IS logged only if the log item is unbound (uninitialized).
The component state logged by a `log` statement IS one of Inactive, Running, Stopped and Killed.
The port state logged by a `log` statement IS one of Started and Stopped.
The default state logged by a `log` statement IS one of Activated and Deactivated.
The timer state logged by a `log` statement IS one of Inactive, Running and Expired.
The logging of the fields of structured values and templates IS NOT standardized, so the logged information of different TTCN-3 tools may differ.
The `log` statement has the syntax `log` followed by a parenthesized sequence of FreeText or TemplateInstance items, each optionally followed by a comma.
The `log` statement writes one or more log items to a logging device associated with the control behaviour or the test component in which the statement is used.
The log items of a `log` statement SHALL be given as a comma-separated list in the argument of the `log` statement.
A log item MAY be an individual language element specified in table 18 or an expression composed of such log items.
The execution of a `log` statement SHOULD have no effect on the test behaviour.
A function used in a `log` statement SHOULD NOT (explicitly or implicitly) change component variable values, port status or timer status.
A function used in a `log` statement SHOULD NOT change the value of any of its `inout` or `out` parameters.
A `break` statement SHALL cause the exit from a loop, from an altstep, or from an `alt` or `interleave` statement.
The `break` statement has the syntax `break`.
A `log` statement MAY contain a formal parameter identifier as a log item.
The logging of an actual parameter SHALL follow the rules specified for the language element it substitutes.
When a value formal parameter identifier is logged, the actual parameter value SHALL be logged.
When a template formal parameter identifier is logged, the actual template or field values and matching symbols SHALL be logged.
When a component type formal parameter identifier is logged, the actual component reference SHALL be logged.
On executing a `break` statement, the innermost, currently executed loop, `alt` statement or `interleave` statement SHALL be left.
After a `break` statement, execution SHALL continue with the statement following the construct which is left.
A `break` statement SHALL NOT be used outside the body of a loop (`for`, `while`, `do-while`) or an alternative of an `alt` or `interleave` statement; such use SHALL cause an error.
An altstep IS always executed within a surrounding `alt` statement.
If the execution of a top alternative of an altstep ends with a `break` statement, the altstep and the surrounding `alt` statement SHALL be left.
When an altstep is left by a `break` statement, execution SHALL continue with the statement following the surrounding `alt` statement.
An optional statement block following an altstep call in an `alt` statement IS NOT executed when the altstep is left by executing a `break` statement.
If the optional statement block following an altstep call has to be executed, the altstep SHALL be left with a `return` statement.
A `continue` statement SHALL cause the start of the next iteration of a loop.
The `continue` statement has the syntax `continue`.
On executing a `continue` statement, the subsequent statements of the body of the innermost, currently executed loop SHALL be skipped.
On executing a `continue` statement, the next iteration of the innermost, currently executed loop SHALL start.
A `continue` statement SHALL NOT be used outside the body of a loop (`for`, `while`, `do-while`); such use SHALL cause an error.
A statement block MAY be used like a basic program statement to introduce a local scope in the flow of control of TTCN-3 behaviour.
The declarations and statements in a statement block SHALL be executed sequentially in the order of their appearance.
A statement block has the syntax "{" followed by any number of LocalDefinition or Statement elements followed by "}".
A statement block IS a local scope unit.
Test behaviour CAN be expressed sequentially, as a set of alternatives, or as a combination of both.
The `interleave` statement CAN specify interleaved sequences or alternatives.
Alternative behaviour IS expressed with the `alt` statement, written `alt { … }`.
Re-evaluation of an `alt` statement IS expressed with the `repeat` statement, written `repeat`.
Interleaved behaviour IS expressed with the `interleave` statement, written `interleave { … }`.
A default IS activated with the `activate` operation, using the keyword `activate`.
A default IS deactivated with the `deactivate` operation, using the keyword `deactivate`.
Sequences of statements CAN be expressed as sets of possible alternatives that form a tree of execution paths.
The `alt` statement IS the statement that expresses sequences of statements as sets of possible alternatives forming a tree of execution paths.
When an `alt` statement is entered, a snapshot IS taken.
A snapshot IS a partial state of a test component.
A snapshot IS including all information necessary to evaluate the Boolean guards of the alternative branches.
A snapshot IS including all relevant stopped test components.
A snapshot IS including all relevant timeout events.
A snapshot IS including the top messages, calls, replies and exceptions in the relevant incoming port queues.
A test component, timer or port that is referenced in at least one alternative of the `alt` statement IS relevant for the snapshot.
A test component, timer or port that is referenced in a top alternative of an altstep invoked as an alternative in the `alt` statement IS relevant for the snapshot.
A test component, timer or port that is referenced in a top alternative of an altstep activated as a default IS relevant for the snapshot.
A snapshot IS only a conceptual means for describing the behaviour of the `alt` statement.
Taking a snapshot IS instantaneous (has no duration) in the TTCN-3 semantics.
In a real implementation, taking a snapshot CAN take some time and race conditions CAN occur.
The handling of race conditions caused by non-instantaneous snapshots IS NOT within the scope of the present document.
An `alt` statement IS a statement that expresses sets of possible alternatives forming a tree of possible execution paths.

An `alt` statement has the syntax `alt` [`@nodefault`] "{" followed by optional local variable, timer, constant or template definitions, followed by alternatives of the form "[" [BooleanExpression] "]" with either a timeout, receive, trigger, getcall, catch, check, getreply, done or killed statement followed by a statement block, or an altstep instance followed by an optional statement block, and an optional final "[" `else` "]" StatementBlock, closed by "}".

An `alt` statement denotes branching of test behaviour due to the reception and handling of communication events, timer events and/or the termination of parallel test components, using the operations `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply`, `catch`, `check`, `timeout`, `done` and `killed`.
An `alt` statement denotes a set of possible events that are matched against a particular snapshot.
An `alt` statement MAY define local definitions before its alternative branches.
A local definition of an `alt` statement CAN be used by all branches of that `alt` statement.
When an `alt` statement is entered, a snapshot IS taken.
If an `alt` statement contains local definitions before its first branch, the local definitions ARE evaluated before the snapshot is taken.
When an `alt` statement executes the `repeat` operation, the whole `alt` statement, including its local definitions, IS re-evaluated.
The alternative branches of an `alt` statement, the top alternatives of invoked altsteps and the top alternatives of altsteps activated as defaults ARE processed in the order of their appearance.
If several defaults are active, the top alternatives of the defaults ARE evaluated in the reverse order of the activation of the defaults.
The alternative branches in active defaults ARE reached by the default mechanism.
If an `alt` statement contains the `@nodefault` modifier, all active default alternatives ARE ignored for the execution of that `alt` statement.
An alternative branch IS either a branch that may be guarded by a Boolean expression or an else-branch, i.e. a branch starting with `[else]`.
An else-branch IS always chosen and executed when it is reached.

A branch that may be guarded by a Boolean expression IS either an altstep-branch (invoking an altstep), a done-branch (starting with a `done` operation), a killed-branch (starting with a `killed` operation), a timeout-branch (starting with a `timeout` operation) or a receiving-branch (starting with a `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply`, `catch` or `check` operation).
The evaluation of a Boolean guard SHALL be based on the snapshot.
A Boolean guard IS considered fulfilled if no Boolean guard is defined or if the Boolean guard evaluates to `true`.
An altstep-branch IS selected if its Boolean guard is fulfilled.
The selection of an altstep-branch causes the invocation of the referenced altstep, and the evaluation of the snapshot continues within the altstep.
An altstep-branch MAY contain an optional statement block.
The optional statement block of an altstep-branch SHALL be executed only if an alternative of the altstep referenced in the altstep-branch has been selected and executed.
A done-branch IS selected if its Boolean guard is fulfilled and the specified test component is in the list of stopped components of the snapshot.
The selection of a done-branch causes the execution of the statement block following the `done` operation.
A `done` operation in a selected done-branch has no further effect beyond the selection of the branch.
A killed-branch IS selected if its Boolean guard is fulfilled and the specified test component is in the list of killed components of the snapshot.
The selection of a killed-branch causes the execution of the statement block following the `killed` operation.
A `killed` operation in a selected killed-branch has no further effect beyond the selection of the branch.
A timeout-branch IS selected if its Boolean guard is fulfilled and the specified timeout event is in the timeout-list of the snapshot.

The selection of a timeout-branch causes the execution of the specified `timeout` operation, i.e. the removal of the timeout event from the timeout-list, and the execution of the statement block following the `timeout` operation.

A receiving-branch IS selected if its Boolean guard is fulfilled and the matching criteria of the receiving operation are fulfilled by one of the messages, calls, replies or exceptions in the snapshot.

The selection of a receiving-branch causes the execution of the receiving operation, i.e. the removal of the matching message, call, reply or exception from the port queue, possibly an assignment of the received information to a variable, and the execution of the statement block following the receiving operation.
In a receiving-branch with a `trigger` operation, the top message of the port queue IS removed also if the Boolean guard is fulfilled but the matching criteria are not.
If the Boolean guard of a `trigger` branch is fulfilled but its matching criteria are not, the statement block of that alternative IS NOT executed.
The evaluation of a snapshot IS described as a series of indivisible actions of a test component.
The TTCN-3 semantics DO NOT assume that the evaluation of a snapshot has no duration.

Events occurring during the evaluation of a snapshot (component stops, timer timeouts, new messages, calls, replies or exceptions entering port queues) DO NOT change the actual snapshot and ARE NOT considered for its evaluation.
Due to dynamic test configurations, a receiving-branch CAN refer to a disconnected or unmapped port at the time of its evaluation.
A port belongs to the receiving component, and matching IS related to the top elements in the port queues.
A dynamically unmapped or disconnected port contributes to a snapshot in the same manner as a mapped or connected port.
The execution of receiving operations MAY empty the queues of unmapped and disconnected ports without causing a test case error.

If none of the alternative branches in an `alt` statement and none of the top alternatives in the invoked altsteps and active defaults can be selected and executed, the `alt` statement SHALL be executed again, i.e. a new snapshot is taken and the evaluation of the alternative branches is repeated with the new snapshot.

The repeated evaluation of an `alt` statement SHALL continue until an alternative branch is selected and executed, the test case is stopped by another component or by the test system, or a dynamic error occurs.
If a test component is completely blocked, the test case SHALL stop and indicate a dynamic error.

A test component IS completely blocked when none of the alternatives can be chosen, no relevant test component is running, no relevant timer is running and all relevant ports contain at least one message, call, reply or exception that does not match.
The repetitive procedure of taking a complete snapshot and re-evaluating all alternatives IS only a conceptual means for describing the semantics of the `alt` statement.
The concrete algorithm that implements the `alt` statement semantics IS outside the scope of the TTCN-3 core language standard.
An alternative MAY be enabled or disabled by a Boolean expression placed between the "[" and "]" brackets of the alternative.
Any branch in an `alt` statement MAY be defined as an else-branch by including the `else` keyword between the opening and closing brackets at the beginning of the alternative.
The statement block of an else-branch IS always executed if no other alternative textually preceding the else-branch has proceeded.
Unless the `@nodefault` modifier is present, the default mechanism IS always invoked at the end of all alternatives of an `alt` statement.
If an else-branch is defined in an `alt` statement, the default mechanism IS NOT called, i.e. active defaults are never entered.
An altstep MAY contain an else-branch.
An else-branch MAY contain a `repeat` statement.
An `alt` statement or an altstep MAY define more than one else-branch.
If an `alt` statement or altstep contains more than one else-branch, only the first else-branch IS ever executed.
The re-evaluation of an `alt` statement CAN be specified by a `repeat` statement.
An altstep MAY be invoked as an alternative in an `alt` statement.
When an altstep is explicitly invoked as an alternative, the optional statement block following the altstep call SHALL also be executed.
Behaviour execution continues with the statement following the `alt` statement when a branch of the `alt` statement or of an invoked default is selected and completely executed.

Behaviour execution continues with the statement following the `alt` statement when a branch of an altstep used in an altstep-branch is selected and both that branch and the optional statement block following the invoked altstep are completely executed.

Execution continues with the statement following the `alt` statement if a `break` statement is reached in the statement block of the selected branch of the `alt` statement, of an altstep used in an altstep-branch, or of an altstep invoked as default.
An `alt` statement MAY be left by a `goto` statement in the selected branch of the `alt` statement, and execution continues with the statement following the label the `goto` points to.
A `goto` statement CANNOT be used to leave an `alt` statement from a branch of an altstep or default.
The open and close square brackets "[" "]" SHALL be present at the start of each alternative of an `alt` statement, even if they are empty.
The mandatory square brackets at the start of each alternative ARE necessary to syntactically distinguish one alternative from another and aid readability.
The evaluation of a Boolean expression guarding an alternative SHALL NOT have side effects.
A Boolean guard expression SHALL obey the same restrictions as the initialization of local definitions within altsteps and the restrictions on the contents of functions called from special places.
The evaluation of the event of an alt branch SHALL NOT have side effects.
An expression occurring in the matching part of an alternative SHALL obey the restrictions on the contents of functions called from special places.
If none of the alternatives of an altstep invoked from an alt branch is chosen, the evaluation of that altstep SHALL NOT have side effects.
An actual parameter of an altstep invoked from an alt branch SHALL obey the restrictions on the contents of functions called from special places.
An `alt` statement used inside control behaviour SHALL only contain timeout statements as alternatives.
A `repeat` statement IS used for a re-evaluation of an `alt` statement.
A `repeat` statement has the syntax `repeat`.

A `repeat` statement in the statement block of an alternative of an `alt` statement causes the re-evaluation of the `alt` statement, i.e. a new snapshot is taken and the alternatives are evaluated in the order of their specification.
A `repeat` statement in a statement block of the response and exception handling part of a blocking procedure call causes the re-evaluation of the response and exception handling part of the call.
A `repeat` statement in a top alternative of an altstep definition causes a new snapshot and the re-evaluation of the `alt` statement from which the altstep has been called.
An altstep containing a `repeat` statement MAY be called either implicitly by the default mechanism or explicitly in an `alt` statement, with the same re-evaluation effect.
A `repeat` statement SHALL only be used within `alt` statements, `call` statements or altsteps.
The `interleave` statement specifies the interleaved occurrence and handling of the receiving events `done`, `killed`, `timeout`, `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply`, `catch` and `check`.

The `interleave` statement has the syntax `interleave [@nodefault] { { [] (TimeoutStatement | ReceiveStatement | TriggerStatement | GetCallStatement | CatchStatement | CheckStatement | GetReplyStatement | DoneStatement | KilledStatement) StatementBlock } }`.

Each branch of an `interleave` statement SHALL start with a reception statement (`timeout`, `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `catch`, `check`, `getreply`, `done` or `killed`) followed by a statement block.
Interleaved behaviour CAN always be replaced by an equivalent set of nested `alt` statements.

Whenever a reception statement within an `interleave` statement is executed, the following non-reception statements ARE executed subsequently until the next reception statement is reached, a `break` statement is reached, or the interleaved sequence ends.
A reception statement IS a TTCN-3 statement that may occur in sets of alternatives, i.e. `receive`, `check`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply`, `catch`, `done`, `killed` and `timeout`.
A non-reception statement IS any other non-control-transfer statement that can be used within the `interleave` statement.
If none of the alternatives of the `interleave` statement can be executed, the default mechanism IS invoked.

When the default mechanism is invoked from an `interleave` statement, the actual snapshot IS used to evaluate the altsteps that have been activated as defaults before entering the `interleave` statement.
If an `interleave` statement contains the `@nodefault` modifier, all active default alternatives ARE ignored for the execution of that `interleave` statement.
The complete semantics of the default mechanism within an `interleave` statement IS given by replacing the `interleave` statement by an equivalent set of nested `alt` statements.
An `interleave` statement with the `@nodefault` modifier IS equivalent to a set of replacement `alt` statements that all have the `@nodefault` modifier.
The default mechanism applies to each of the replacement `alt` statements of an `interleave` statement.
If no `break` statement was encountered, the evaluation of the `interleave` statement continues by taking the next snapshot.
The evaluation of an `interleave` statement IS terminated if a `break` statement is executed.

An `interleave` statement SHALL NOT contain the control transfer statements `activate`, `deactivate`, `repeat`, any call of an altstep, or any direct or indirect call of a user-defined function that includes reception statements.
A branch of an `interleave` statement SHALL NOT be guarded by a Boolean expression, i.e. the `[ ]` SHALL always be empty.
An `interleave` statement SHALL NOT contain an `else` branch.
An `interleave` statement used inside control behaviour SHALL only contain `timeout` statements in the event parts of its alternatives.
The control transfer statements `for`, `while`, `do-while` and `goto` MAY be used within `interleave` statements under the conditions stated in 20.4 restriction d).
The loop statements `for`, `while` and `do-while` MAY be used within an `interleave` statement only in statement blocks that do not contain reception statements.
A `for`, `while` or `do-while` statement SHALL NOT be used within an `interleave` statement in a statement block that contains reception statements.
A `goto` statement MAY be used within an `interleave` statement for jumps within statement blocks that do not contain reception statements.
A `goto` statement MAY be used to jump out of an `interleave` statement.
An altstep MAY be activated as a default.
Each test component stores its defaults, i.e. its activated altsteps, as an ordered list.
The list of defaults IS ordered in reverse order of activation, i.e. the last activated default is the first element in the list.
The `activate` and `deactivate` operations operate on the list of defaults.
If an `activate` operation creates a new default, the new default IS inserted as the first element into the list of defaults.
A re-activated default that was previously suspended retains its position in the list of defaults.
The `deactivate` operation either removes a default from the list of defaults or suspends it, in which case the default remains in the list but is temporarily inactive.
A default in the list of defaults IS identified by a default reference generated as the result of the corresponding `activate` operation.
The default mechanism IS evoked at the end of each `alt` statement not annotated with the `@nodefault` modifier, if due to the actual snapshot none of the specified alternatives could be executed.
The default mechanism IS NOT evoked at the end of an `alt` statement annotated with the `@nodefault` modifier.
An evoked default mechanism invokes the first altstep in the list of defaults, i.e. the last activated default, and waits for the result of its termination.
The termination of a default invoked by the default mechanism IS either successful or unsuccessful.
The termination of a default IS unsuccessful if none of the top alternatives of the altstep defining the default behaviour could be selected.
The termination of a default IS successful if one of the top alternatives of the default has been selected and executed.
An `interleave` statement IS semantically equivalent to a nested set of `alt` statements, and the default mechanism applies to each of these `alt` statements.
The default mechanism applies to `interleave` statements.
The restrictions imposed on `interleave` statements in clause 20.4 do not apply to altsteps activated as default behaviour for `interleave` statements.
An alternative in an altstep activated as a default CAN refer to a disconnected or unmapped port at the time of its evaluation.
A port belongs to the receiving component, and matching relates to the top elements of the port queues.
A dynamically unmapped or disconnected port contributes to a snapshot in the same manner as a mapped or connected port.
An altstep invoked as a default CAN execute receiving operations that empty the queues of unmapped or disconnected ports without causing a test case error.
In the case of an unsuccessful termination of a default, the default mechanism invokes the next default in the list of defaults that is not in the suspended state.

If the last default in the list of defaults has terminated unsuccessfully, the default mechanism returns to the end of the `alt` statement in which it was invoked and indicates an unsuccessful default execution.
The default mechanism indicates an unsuccessful default execution if the list of defaults is empty or contains only suspended defaults.
An unsuccessful default execution causes a new snapshot to be taken, or a dynamic error if the test component is blocked.
After a successful termination, a default CAN stop the test component by means of a `stop` statement.

After a successful termination of a default that does not stop the test component, the main control flow of the test component either continues immediately after the `alt` statement from which the default mechanism was called, or the test component takes a new snapshot and re-evaluates the `alt` statement.
Re-evaluation of the `alt` statement after a successful default termination SHALL be specified by means of a `repeat` statement in the default.

If the execution of the selected top alternative of a default ends with a `break` statement or without a `repeat` statement, the control flow of the test component continues immediately after the `alt` statement.
The TTCN-3 language does not restrict the implementation of the default mechanism.
