A TTCN-3 tool MAY implement the default mechanism as a process implicitly called at the end of each `alt` statement or as a separate thread responsible for default handling.
When the default mechanism has been invoked, the defaults SHALL be called in the reverse order of their activation.
The `activate` operation IS used to activate altsteps as defaults.
The `activate` operation has the syntax `activate ( AltstepRef ( [ActualPar {, ActualPar}] ) | ObjectReference )`.
An `activate` operation called with an AltstepRef puts the referenced altstep as the first element into the list of defaults.
An `activate` operation called with an AltstepRef returns a default reference.
A default reference IS a unique identifier for the default.
A default reference MAY be used in a `deactivate` operation to deactivate the default.
The actual parameters of a parameterized altstep that is activated as a default SHALL be provided in the corresponding `activate` operation.
The actual parameters of an altstep activated as a default ARE bound to the default at the time of its activation, not at the time of its invocation by the default mechanism.
An `activate` operation called with an ObjectReference re-activates the referenced default that was previously suspended by a `deactivate` operation.
A default re-activated by an `activate` operation with an ObjectReference SHALL remain in the same place in the list of defaults as before the `activate` operation.
An `activate` operation called with an ObjectReference SHALL return the same ObjectReference as it received at calling.
The effect of an `activate` operation IS local to the test component in which it is called.
A test component CANNOT activate a default in another test component.
An `activate` operation MAY be called without saving the returned default reference.
A default that is not explicitly deactivated IS deactivated implicitly at MTC termination.
An altstep that is activated as a default SHALL only have `in` formal parameters.
The ObjectReference of an `activate` operation SHALL be of `default` type.
The ObjectReference of an `activate` operation SHALL refer to a default that is marked as suspended in the list of defaults.
The `deactivate` operation IS used to deactivate or suspend defaults, i.e. previously activated altsteps.
The `deactivate` operation has the syntax `deactivate [ ( ObjectReference [, Expression] ) ]`.
If the optional Expression evaluates to `false`, a `deactivate` operation removes the referenced default from the list of defaults.
If the optional Expression evaluates to `true`, a `deactivate` operation marks the referenced default in the list of defaults as suspended.
A suspended default CAN be re-activated by an `activate` operation.
The effect of a `deactivate` operation IS local to the test component in which it is called.
A test component CANNOT deactivate or suspend a default in another test component.
A `deactivate` operation without parameters deactivates all defaults of the test component.
A `deactivate` operation called with the special value `null` as its ObjectReference has no effect.
A `deactivate` operation called with an undefined default reference, e.g. a reference to an already deactivated default or an uninitialized default reference variable, SHALL cause a runtime error.
The ObjectReference of a `deactivate` operation SHALL be of `default` type.
The optional Expression of a `deactivate` operation SHALL be of `boolean` type.
The optional Expression of a `deactivate` operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The default value of the optional Expression of a `deactivate` operation IS `false`.
The optional Expression of a `deactivate` operation SHALL evaluate to an initialized value.
A configuration operation IS an operation used to set up and control test components and their connections.
A configuration operation SHALL only be used in a test case, or in behaviour invoked directly or indirectly from a test case or from behaviour started on a PTC.
A configuration operation SHALL NOT be used in control behaviour.
A configuration operation SHALL NOT be used in a declaration inside a component type definition.
A configuration operation SHALL NOT be used in a function invoked directly or indirectly from a declaration inside a component type definition.
The `connect` operation IS connecting a port of one test component to a port of another test component.
The `connect` operation has the syntax `connect(ComponentRef:Port, ComponentRef:Port)`, e.g. `connect(ptc1:p1, ptc2:p2);`.
The `disconnect` operation IS disconnecting two or more connected ports.
The `disconnect` operation has the syntax `disconnect(ComponentRef:Port, ComponentRef:Port)`, e.g. `disconnect(ptc1:p1, ptc2:p2);`.
The `map` operation IS mapping a port of one test component to a port of the test system interface.
The `map` operation has the syntax `map(ComponentRef:Port, system:Port)`, e.g. `map(ptc1:q, system:sutPort1);`.
The `unmap` operation IS unmapping two or more mapped ports.
The `unmap` operation has the syntax `unmap(ComponentRef:Port, system:Port)`, e.g. `unmap(ptc1:q, system:sutPort1);`.
The `create` operation IS creating a normal (non-alive) or an alive test component.
The distinction between a normal and an alive test component IS made when the test component is created.
The MTC IS behaving as a normal (non-alive) test component.
The `create` operation has the syntax `ComponentType.create` for non-alive and `ComponentType.create alive` for alive test components, e.g. `var PTCType c := PTCType.create alive;`.
The `start` test component operation IS starting test behaviour on a test component.
Starting behaviour on a test component IS NOT affecting the status of the component variables, component timers or component ports of that test component.
The `start` test component operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.start(FunctionInstance)`, e.g. `c.start(PTCBehaviour());`.
The `stop` test component operation IS stopping the test behaviour running on a test component.
The `stop` test component operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.stop`, e.g. `c.stop;`.
The `kill` test component operation IS causing a test component to cease to exist.
The `kill` test component operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.kill`, e.g. `c.kill;`.
The `alive` operation IS returning `true` if the test component has been created and is ready to execute or is already executing behaviour.
The `alive` operation IS returning `false` if the test component has not been created, or is neither ready to execute nor executing behaviour.
The `alive` operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.alive` and is a Boolean expression, e.g. `if (c.alive) …`.
The `running` test component operation IS returning `true` as long as the test component is executing behaviour.
The `running` test component operation IS returning `false` when the test component is not executing behaviour.
The `running` test component operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.running` and is a Boolean expression, e.g. `if (c.running) …`.
The `done` operation IS checking whether the function running on a test component has terminated.
The `done` operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.done`, e.g. `c.done;`.
The `killed` operation IS checking whether a test component has ceased to exist.
The `killed` operation has the syntax `ComponentRef.killed`, e.g. `c.killed { … }` as an alternative.
The `testcase.stop` operation IS terminating the test case with the test verdict `error`.
The `testcase.stop` operation has the syntax `testcase.stop(…)` with an optional log argument list, e.g. `testcase.stop ( … );`.
The `mtc` operation IS returning the reference to the MTC.
The `mtc` operation has the syntax `mtc`, usable as a component reference, e.g. `connect(mtc:p, ptc:p);`.
The `system` operation IS returning the reference to the test system interface.
The `system` operation has the syntax `system`, usable as a component reference, e.g. `map(c:p, system:sutPort);`.
The `self` operation IS returning the reference to the test component that executes the `self` operation.
The `self` operation has the syntax `self`, usable as a component reference, e.g. `self.stop;`.
A port of a test component CAN be connected to ports of other test components or to ports of the test system interface.
For a connection between two test components, the `connect` operation SHALL be used.
When connecting a test component to the test system interface, the `map` operation SHALL be used.
The `connect` operation directly connects one port to another port, with the in side of each port connected to the out side of the other port.
The `map` operation IS a name translation defining how communication streams can be referenced.
The `create` operation creates a normal or an alive test component.
The distinction between a normal and an alive test component IS made during the creation of the test component.
The MTC behaves as a normal test component.
The `create` operation has the syntax ComponentType.create for a non-alive test component and ComponentType.create alive for an alive test component.
The `start` test component operation starts test behaviour on a test component.
Starting behaviour on a test component does not affect the status of the component variables, component timers or ports of that test component.
The `start` test component operation has the syntax ComponentRef.start(FunctionInstance), e.g. c.start(PTCBehaviour()).
The `stop` test component operation stops test behaviour on a test component.
The `stop` test component operation has the syntax ComponentRef.stop, e.g. c.stop.
The `kill` operation causes a test component to cease to exist.
The `kill` operation has the syntax ComponentRef.kill, e.g. c.kill.
The `alive` operation returns true if the test component has been created and is ready to execute or is already executing behaviour.
The `alive` operation returns false if the test component has not been created or is not ready to execute and is not executing behaviour.
The `alive` operation has the syntax ComponentRef.alive and is a boolean expression, e.g. if (c.alive).
The `running` operation returns true as long as the test component is executing behaviour.
The `running` operation returns false when the test component is not executing behaviour.
The `running` operation has the syntax ComponentRef.running and is a boolean expression, e.g. if (c.running).
The `done` operation checks whether the function running on a test component has terminated.
The `done` operation has the syntax ComponentRef.done, e.g. c.done.
The `killed` operation checks whether a test component has ceased to exist.
The `killed` operation has the syntax ComponentRef.killed, e.g. c.killed.
The `testcase.stop` operation terminates the test case with the test verdict `error`.
The test case stop operation has the syntax testcase.stop ( ... ).
The `mtc` operation returns the component reference of the MTC.
The `mtc` operation is written as the keyword `mtc` and can be used as a component reference in a port reference, e.g. connect(mtc:p, ptc:p).
The `system` operation returns the reference to the test system interface.
The `system` operation is written as the keyword `system` and can be used as a component reference in a port reference, e.g. map(c:p, system:sutPort).
The `self` operation returns the component reference of the test component that executes the `self` operation.
The `self` operation is written as the keyword `self` and can be used as a component reference, e.g. self.stop.
The `connect` operation sets up a connection between ports of test components.
The `map` operation sets up a mapping between a port of a test component and a port of the test system interface towards the SUT.
The `connect` operation has the syntax connect ( ComponentRef : Port , ComponentRef : Port ).
The `map` operation has the syntax map ( ComponentRef : Port , ComponentRef : Port ) optionally followed by a param clause param ( [ ActualPar { , ActualPar } ] ).
In a `connect` or `map` operation, each port to be connected IS identified by the component reference of its component and the port name.
The `mtc` operation identifies the MTC.
The `system` operation identifies the test system interface.
The `self` operation identifies the test component in which `self` has been called.
The `mtc`, `system` and `self` operations MAY be used as component references for identifying and connecting ports.
The `connect` operation SHALL only be invoked from the places specified in clause 21.0.
The `map` operation SHALL only be invoked from the places specified in clause 21.0.
Before a `connect` or `map` operation is called, the test components to be connected SHALL have been created.
Before a `connect` or `map` operation is called, the component references of the test components to be connected and the names of the relevant ports SHALL be known.

Applying a `connect` or `map` operation to ports which are already connected or mapped to each other has no effect on the test behaviour or test configuration, and test execution continues as if the operation had not been invoked.
When a `map` or `connect` operation is applied to ports that are already mapped or connected, triMap or tciConnect respectively is not invoked.
A `map` operation MAY contain an optional parameter list (param clause) for configuration purposes.
The param clause of a `map` operation allows passing values needed for dynamic runtime configuration.
If a param clause is present in a `map` operation, its actual parameters SHALL conform to the map param clause of the port type declaration of the system port used.
A `connect` or `map` operation SHALL only establish consistent connections.
In the consistency rules for `connect` and `map`, PORT1 and PORT2 denote the two ports to be connected or mapped.
inlist-PORT1 denotes the messages or procedures of the in-direction of PORT1.
outlist-PORT1 denotes the messages or procedures of the out-direction of PORT1.
inlist-PORT2 denotes the messages or procedures of the in-direction of PORT2.
outlist-PORT2 denotes the messages or procedures of the out-direction of PORT2.

A `connect` operation MAY be applied if outlist-PORT1 ⊆ inlist-PORT2, outlist-PORT2 ⊆ inlist-PORT1, neither PORT1 nor PORT2 is a system port reference, and at least one of outlist-PORT1 or outlist-PORT2 is not empty.
In a `connect` operation, outlist-PORT1 SHALL be a subset of inlist-PORT2.
In a `connect` operation, outlist-PORT2 SHALL be a subset of inlist-PORT1.
Neither port of a `connect` operation SHALL be a system port reference.
In a `connect` operation, at least one of outlist-PORT1 or outlist-PORT2 SHALL NOT be empty.

A `map` operation MAY be applied if one port is a component port reference and the other a system port reference, outlist-PORT1 ⊆ outlist-PORT2, inlist-PORT2 ⊆ inlist-PORT1, and at least one of outlist-PORT1 or inlist-PORT2 is not empty.
In a `map` operation, one port (PORT1) SHALL be a component port reference and the other port (PORT2) SHALL be a system port reference.
In a `map` operation, outlist-PORT1 of the component port SHALL be a subset of outlist-PORT2 of the system port.
In a `map` operation, inlist-PORT2 of the system port SHALL be a subset of inlist-PORT1 of the component port.
In a `map` operation, at least one of outlist-PORT1 or inlist-PORT2 SHALL NOT be empty.
The system port CAN be either the first or the second operand of a `map` operation.
A `connect` operation that does not satisfy the conditions of restriction b) SHALL NOT be allowed.
A `map` operation that does not satisfy the conditions of restriction c) SHALL NOT be allowed.
Because TTCN-3 allows dynamic configurations and addresses, not all consistency checks for `connect` and `map` can be made statically at compile time.
A consistency check for `connect` or `map` that cannot be made at compile time SHALL be made at runtime.
A failing runtime consistency check for `connect` or `map` SHALL lead to a test case error.
The restrictions on allowed and disallowed connections described in clause 9.1 SHALL apply to `connect` and `map` operations.
A `map` operation MAY omit the param clause.
If a `map` operation has a param clause, exactly one of the components referenced by the operation SHALL be the system component reference.

If a `map` operation has a param clause, the type of the system component SHALL be known in the context of the operation, either via a system clause or via the runs on clause of a testcase without system clause.
If a `map` operation has a param clause, the type of the system port to which the operation is applied SHALL include a map param declaration.
If a `map` operation has a param clause, its actual parameters SHALL conform to the map param clause of the port type declaration of the system port used.

If the type of a component referenced in a `connect` or `map` operation is known (the component reference is a variable or a value returned from a function, or the type is defined in the runs on, mtc or system clause of the calling function), the referenced port SHALL be declared in that component type.
The `disconnect` operation IS the opposite operation of the `connect` operation.
The `unmap` operation IS the opposite operation of the `map` operation.

The `disconnect` operation has the syntax disconnect optionally followed by one of ( ComponentRef : Port , ComponentRef : Port ), ( PortRef ), ( ComponentRef : all port ) or ( all component : all port ).

The `unmap` operation has the syntax unmap optionally followed by one of ( ComponentRef : Port , ComponentRef : Port ) [param clause], ( PortRef ) [param clause], ( ComponentRef : all port ) or ( all component : all port ).
The `disconnect` operation disconnects previously connected ports of test components.
The `unmap` operation unmaps previously mapped ports of test components and ports of the test system interface.
A `disconnect` operation MAY be called from any test component if the relevant component references and the names of the relevant ports are known.
An `unmap` operation MAY be called from any test component if the relevant component references and the names of the relevant ports are known.
A `disconnect` or `unmap` operation has an effect only if the connection or mapping to be removed has been created beforehand; otherwise it has no effect.
A `disconnect` or `unmap` operation MAY be used with one argument only, to address all connections or mappings of a component or a port.
The single argument of a `disconnect` or `unmap` operation specifies one side of the connections or mappings to be removed, and all connections or mappings of that side are removed.
The `all port` keyword MAY be used in a `disconnect` or `unmap` operation to denote all ports of a component.
A `disconnect` or `unmap` operation without any parameters IS a shorthand form for the same operation with the parameter self:all port.
A `disconnect` or `unmap` operation without parameters disconnects or unmaps all ports of the test component that calls the operation.
The `all component` keyword SHALL only be used in combination with the `all port` keyword, i.e. as all component:all port.
The `all component` keyword SHALL only be used by the MTC.
The all component:all port argument SHALL be the one and only argument of a `disconnect` or `unmap` operation.
A `disconnect` or `unmap` operation with the argument all component:all port releases all connections or mappings of the test configuration.
An `unmap` operation MAY contain an optional parameter list (param clause) for configuration purposes.
If a param clause is present in an `unmap` operation, its actual parameters SHALL conform to the unmap param clause of the port type declaration of the system port used.
The param clause of an `unmap` operation allows passing values needed for dynamic runtime configuration.
In an `unmap` operation, a param clause SHALL only be present if the system port to which the param clause belongs is explicitly referenced.
An `unmap` operation MAY omit the param clause.
If an `unmap` operation has a param clause, exactly one of the components referenced by the operation SHALL be the system component reference.

If an `unmap` operation has a param clause, the type of the system component SHALL be known in the context of the operation, either via a system clause or via the runs on clause of a testcase without system clause.
If an `unmap` operation has a param clause, the type of the system port to which the operation is applied SHALL include an unmap param declaration.
If an `unmap` operation has a param clause, its actual parameters SHALL conform to the unmap param clause of the port type declaration of the system port used.

If the type of a component referenced in a `disconnect` or `unmap` operation is known (the component reference is a variable or a value returned from a function, or the type is defined in the runs on, mtc or system clause of the calling function), the referenced port SHALL be declared in that component type.
The parameters of a `disconnect` operation SHALL NOT contain a system port reference.
A test case operation addresses the entire test case by using the keyword `testcase`.
The test case stop operation IS the only test case operation.
The test case stop operation specifies an immediate stop of the test case behaviour with the verdict `error`.
The test case stop operation causes a user-defined immediate termination of a test case with the test verdict `error`.
The test case stop operation MAY specify an optional reason for the termination.
The test case stop operation IS intended for cases where user-defined behaviour that does not contribute to the test outcome behaves unexpectedly so that continuing the test case makes no sense.
The test case stop operation has the syntax testcase . stop optionally followed by a parenthesized comma-separated list of FreeText or TemplateInstance items.
The test case stop operation causes an immediate stop of the entire test case behaviour with the verdict `error`.

The test case stop operation writes the items in its argument, specifying the reason for the termination, to a logging device associated with the test control or the test component in which the operation is used.
The items to be logged by a test case stop operation SHALL be given as a comma-separated list in the argument of the operation.
The argument of the test case stop operation SHALL follow the same restrictions as the argument of the `log` statement.
Test component operations are used to create, start, stop and kill test components.
Test component operations are also used to check whether test components are alive, running, done or killed.
The `create` operation IS the operation used to create test components.
The `create` operation has the syntax ComponentType "." `create` [ "(" Expression ["," Expression] ")" ] [ `alive` ].
The MTC IS the only test component that is created automatically when a test case starts.
A PTC SHALL be created explicitly during test execution by a `create` operation.
A newly created test component IS created with its full set of ports, the input queues of which are empty.
A newly created test component IS created with its full set of component constants, component variables and component timers.
A port whose port type allows incoming (in or inout) communication SHALL be in a listening state, ready to receive traffic over the connection, when the component is created.
When a test component is explicitly or implicitly created, every component variable and component timer IS reset to its initial value, if any.
When a test component is explicitly or implicitly created, every component constant IS reset to its assigned value.

A PTC IS either a non-alive PTC, which can execute a behaviour only once, or an alive-type PTC, which is kept alive after termination of a behaviour and can therefore be reused to execute another behaviour.
An alive-type PTC IS created using the `create` operation with the additional `alive` keyword.
An alive-type PTC SHALL be destroyed explicitly using the `kill` operation.
A non-alive PTC IS destroyed implicitly after its behaviour terminates.
The termination of a test case, i.e. of the MTC, terminates all PTCs that still exist.
A test case SHALL completely create its required configuration of test components and connections when it is invoked.
Every test component and every port IS implicitly destroyed at the termination of each test case.
The `create` operation SHALL return the unique component reference of the newly created test component instance.
A component reference returned by the `create` operation CAN be stored in a variable.
A component reference CAN be used for connecting test component instances and for communication purposes such as sending and receiving.
A name MAY be associated with a newly created test component instance.
The test system SHALL automatically associate the name 'MTC' with the MTC at its creation.
The test system SHALL automatically associate the name 'SYSTEM' with the test system interface at its creation.
An associated component instance name NEED NOT be unique.
A component instance name IS used for logging purposes only.
A component instance name SHALL NOT be used to refer to the component instance.
The component reference SHALL be used to refer to a component instance.
A component instance name IS NOT considered in matching.
A host id MAY be associated with a newly created test component instance.
If a host id is provided and the component cannot be deployed on the specified host, the `create` operation SHALL cause a test case error.
The `create` operation MAY be used at any point in a behaviour definition.
Any test component MAY create any other PTC.
The visibility of a component reference SHALL follow the same scope rules as the visibility of variables.
To reference a test component outside the scope of its creation, the component reference SHALL be passed as a parameter or as a field in a message.
The name given by the first Expression of the `create` operation SHALL be a `charstring` value.
When a component name is assigned, it SHALL appear as the first argument of the `create` operation.
The host id given by the second Expression of the `create` operation SHALL be a `charstring` value.
When a host id is assigned, it SHALL appear as the second argument of the `create` operation.
The start test component operation IS the operation used to associate a test behaviour with a test component, which then executes that behaviour.
The start test component operation has the syntax ObjectReference "." `start` "(" ( FunctionInstance | AltstepInstance ) ")".
Once a PTC has been created, a behaviour SHALL be bound to the PTC and its execution SHALL be started.
Binding a behaviour to a PTC and starting its execution IS done by the start test component operation.
The creation of a PTC IS NOT the start of the execution of the component behaviour.
The start test component operation SHALL bind the required behaviour to the test component.
The behaviour started on a test component IS defined by reference to an already defined function or altstep.
An alive-type PTC MAY perform several behaviours in sequential order.
Starting a second behaviour on a non-alive PTC IS a test case error.
Starting a behaviour on a PTC that is still running IS a test case error.

A behaviour started on an alive-type PTC after termination of a previous behaviour IS executed with the variable values, timers, ports and local verdict as they were left after termination of the previous behaviour.
If a timer was started in the previous behaviour of an alive-type PTC, the subsequent behaviour SHOULD be enabled to handle a possible timeout event.
Every active default IS deactivated when the behaviour of an alive-type PTC is stopped.
When a new behaviour is started on an alive-type PTC, a default IS NOT active.
The lifetime of a variable or timer IS bound to the scope in which it is declared.
When an alive-type component is stopped, only the component scope remains.

A behaviour with a corresponding runs on clause started on an alive-type PTC CAN access only the variable values and timers declared in the component type definition of that PTC from previous behaviours.
In a start test component operation, an actual inout parameter IS passed to the started function by value, i.e. like an in parameter.
In a start test component operation, an actual out parameter MAY be omitted using the not-used symbol ("-").
In a start test component operation using list notation, an actual out parameter MAY be omitted if all following actual parameters are also omitted.
In a start test component operation using assignment notation, the assignment of an actual out parameter MAY be omitted altogether.
A variable given as an actual out parameter in a start test component operation IS left unchanged by the started behaviour, even if the behaviour changes the formal parameter during its execution.
A return value or out or inout parameter of a function invoked in a start test component operation IS NOT effective when the started test component terminates.
The ObjectReference of a start test component operation SHALL be of component type.
The ObjectReference of a start test component operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.

A function or altstep invoked in a start test component operation SHALL have a runs on clause referencing a component type that is compatible with the test component referenced by the ObjectReference.
Every formal parameter of a function or altstep invoked in a start test component operation SHALL be of a component data type.
When a test component starts execution, messages CAN already be waiting in the incoming queues of its in and inout ports, because these ports start listening when the component is created.
The stop test behaviour operation IS the operation used to stop the execution of a test component by itself or by another test component.
The stop test behaviour operation has the syntax `stop` | ( ( ObjectReference | `mtc` | `self` ) "." `stop` ) | ( `all component` "." `stop` ).
A test component CAN stop the execution of its own currently running test behaviour or of the test behaviour running on another test component by using the `stop` operation.
When a test component stops the behaviour running on another test component, the component to be stopped SHALL be identified by its component reference.
A test component MAY stop its own behaviour by a simple `stop` execution statement or by addressing itself in the `stop` operation, e.g. with `self.stop`.
Each of the `create`, `start`, `running`, `done` and `killed` operations IS applicable to PTCs only.
The `stop` operation CAN also be applied to the MTC.
Stopping a test component IS the explicit form of terminating the execution of its currently running behaviour.
A test component behaviour IS also terminated when its execution reaches the end of the test behaviour started on the component or an explicit `return` statement.
Termination of a test component behaviour by reaching its end or by an explicit `return` statement IS called implicit stop.
An implicit stop IS equivalent in its effects to an explicit stop.
When a test component stops (implicitly or explicitly), the global verdict IS updated with the local verdict of the stopped test component.
If the stopped test component is the MTC, the resources of all existing PTCs SHALL be released.
If the stopped test component is the MTC, all existing PTCs SHALL be removed from the test system.
If the stopped test component is the MTC, the test case SHALL terminate.
Stopping a non-alive-type test component (implicitly or explicitly) SHALL destroy it.
When a non-alive-type test component is stopped, all resources associated with it SHALL be released.
Stopping an alive-type component SHALL stop only its currently running behaviour.
A stopped alive-type component SHALL continue to exist.
A stopped alive-type component CAN execute a new behaviour started on it by the start test component operation.
When an alive-type component is stopped, every component variable, component timer and port IS unchanged in its value, contents or state.
When an alive-type component is stopped, its local verdict IS kept unchanged.
When an alive-type component is stopped, every active default IS automatically deactivated.
A test component SHALL be left in a consistent state after its behaviour is stopped.

If the behaviour of an alive-type component is stopped while a new value is assigned to an already bound variable, the variable SHALL remain bound after the component is stopped (with the old or the new value).
If an alive-type component is stopped while re-starting an already running timer, the timer SHALL be left in the running state after termination of the behaviour.
The `all component` keyword SHALL be used with the `stop` operation by the MTC only.
The `all component.stop` operation IS the stopping of every running PTC, excluding the MTC itself.
A PTC CAN stop the test case execution by stopping the MTC.
The ObjectReference of a stop test behaviour operation SHALL be of component type.
The ObjectReference of a stop test behaviour operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The kill test component operation IS the operation used to destroy a test component by itself or by another test component.
On a non-alive test component, the `kill` operation IS equivalent in its results to the `stop` operation.
Stopping an alive-type component IS the termination of its test behaviour only, while the test component continues to exist.
Killing a test component IS the destruction of that test component.
The kill test component operation has the syntax `kill` | ( ( ObjectReference | `mtc` | `self` ) "." `kill` ) | ( `all component` "." `kill` ).
The `kill` operation applied on a test component IS terminating the execution of the currently running behaviour of that component, if any.
The `kill` operation applied on a test component IS freeing all resources associated with that component, including all its port connections.
The `kill` operation applied on a test component IS removing the component from the test system.
The `kill` operation MAY be applied by a test component on itself by a simple `kill` statement or by `self.kill`.
The `kill` operation MAY be applied to another test component.
When the `kill` operation is applied to another test component, the component to be killed SHALL be addressed using its component reference.
If the `kill` operation is applied on the MTC (e.g. `mtc.kill`), the test case IS terminated.
The `all component` keyword SHALL be used with the `kill` operation by the MTC only.
The `all component.kill` operation IS stopping and killing every PTC, excluding the MTC itself.
The ObjectReference of a kill test component operation SHALL be of component type.
The ObjectReference of a kill test component operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The `alive` operation IS a Boolean operation that checks whether a test component has been created and is ready to execute or is already executing a behaviour.
The `alive` operation has the syntax ( ObjectReference | `any component` | `all component` | `any from` ComponentArrayRef ) "." `alive` [ "->" `@index` `value` ValueRef ].
Applied on a non-alive PTC, the `alive` operation IS true if the component is inactive or running a behaviour.
Applied on a non-alive PTC that is neither inactive nor running a behaviour, the `alive` operation IS false.
Applied on an alive-type PTC, the `alive` operation IS true if the component is inactive, running or stopped.
Applied on an alive-type PTC that has been killed, the `alive` operation IS false.
Applied on the MTC, the `alive` operation IS true.
The `alive` operation CAN be used similarly to the `running` operation.
The `all component.alive` operation IS true if all PTCs (alive-type or non-alive) are alive.
The `any component.alive` operation IS true if at least one PTC is alive.

When the `any from` component array notation is used with the `alive` operation, each component of the referenced array IS checked in turn, iterating from innermost to outermost dimension and from lowest to highest index for each dimension.
When the `any from` component array notation is used, the `alive` operation IS true as soon as the first component found inactive or running a behaviour is reached.

The index of the first component found alive MAY be assigned to an integer variable for a single-dimensional component array, or to an integer array or record of integer variable for a multi-dimensional component array.
The ObjectReference of an `alive` operation SHALL be of component type.
The ObjectReference of an `alive` operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The ComponentArrayRef of an `alive` operation SHALL be a reference to a completely initialized component array.
The index redirection of an `alive` operation SHALL only be used when the operation is applied on an `any from` component array construct.
If the index redirection is used for a single-dimensional component array, the type of the integer variable SHALL allow storing the highest index of the array.
If the index redirection is used for a multi-dimensional component array, the size of the integer array or record of integer type SHALL be exactly the same as the dimension of the array.

If the index redirection is used for a multi-dimensional component array, the element type of the integer array or record of integer variable SHALL allow storing the highest index (from all dimensions) of the array.

If a variable referenced in the `@index` clause of an `alive` operation is a lazy or fuzzy variable, the index value assigned to it IS the value produced by the `alive` operation; a later evaluation of the variable does not invoke the `alive` operation again.
The `running` operation IS a Boolean operation that checks whether a test component is already executing a behaviour.
The `running` operation has the syntax ( ObjectReference | `any component` | `all component` | `any from` ComponentArrayRef ) "." `running` [ "->" `@index` `value` ValueRef ].
The `running` operation CAN be used by behaviour executing on a test component to ascertain whether behaviour running on a different test component has completed.
The `running` operation returns `true` for the MTC and for a PTC that has been started but not yet terminated or stopped.
The `running` operation returns `false` for a test component that has not been started or has already terminated or been stopped.
The `running` operation IS a boolean expression that returns a boolean value indicating whether the specified test component (or all test components) is still executing.
In contrast to the `done` operation, the `running` operation MAY be used freely in boolean expressions.
`all component.running` returns `true` if all PTCs that have been started but not stopped explicitly by another component are executing their behaviour.
`all component.running` returns `false` if not all PTCs started but not stopped explicitly by another component are executing their behaviour.
`ptc.running` IS `false` for a PTC that has never been started, while `all component.running` can be `true` at the same time because it considers only PTCs that have been started.
`any component.running` returns `true` if at least one PTC is executing its behaviour.
`any component.running` returns `false` if no PTC is executing its behaviour.

When the `any from` component array notation is used with the `running` operation, each component of the referenced array IS checked individually for executing, iterating from innermost to outermost dimension and from lowest to highest index within each dimension.
With the `any from` component array notation, the first component found executing causes the `running` operation to succeed.

The index of the component matched by the `running` operation with `any from` MAY be assigned to an integer variable for a single-dimensional component array, or to an integer array or record of integer variable for a multi-dimensional component array.
The ObjectReference of the `running` operation SHALL be of a component type.
The ObjectReference of the `running` operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The ComponentArrayRef of the `running` operation SHALL be a reference to a completely initialized component array.
The index redirection of the `running` operation SHALL only be used when the operation is applied to an `any from` component array construct.
The type of the integer variable used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of the single-dimensional component array.
The size of the integer array or record of integer type used in the index redirection SHALL be exactly the same as the number of dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
The element type of the integer array or record of integer used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of all dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
If a variable referenced in the @index clause is a lazy or fuzzy variable, the expression assigned to that variable IS equal to the result produced by the `running` operation.
Later evaluation of a lazy or fuzzy variable referenced in the @index clause IS NOT a repeated invocation of the `running` operation.
The `done` operation CAN be used by behaviour executing on a test component to ascertain whether the behaviour running on a different test component has completed.
The `done` operation CAN retrieve the final local verdict of a completed test component.
The final local verdict of a test component IS the value of its local verdict at the time of test component completion.

The `done` operation has the syntax [ `@nodefault` ] ( ObjectReference | `any component` | `all component` | `any from` ComponentArrayRef ) "." `done` [ "->" [ `value` ValueRef ] [ `@index` `value` ValueRef ] ].
The `done` operation SHALL be used in the same manner as a receiving operation or a timeout operation.
The `done` operation SHALL NOT be used in a boolean expression.
The `done` operation MAY be used to determine an alternative in an `alt` statement.
The `done` operation MAY be used as a stand-alone statement in a behaviour description.
A stand-alone `done` operation IS a shorthand for an `alt` statement with the `done` operation as the only alternative.
If the `@nodefault` modifier is placed before a stand-alone `done` operation, the implicit `alt` statement IS also qualified with the `@nodefault` modifier.
A `done` operation applied to a PTC matches only if the behaviour of that PTC has been stopped (implicitly or explicitly) or the PTC has been killed.
A `done` operation applied to a PTC whose behaviour has not been stopped and which has not been killed IS unsuccessful.
The execution of a `done` operation does not change the state of the test component.
Consecutive `done` operations applied to the same test component give the same result as long as the test component does not change its state.
When a `done` operation applied to a PTC matches, the final local verdict of the PTC MAY be retrieved and stored in a variable of type `verdicttype`.
Storing the final local verdict IS denoted by the symbol "->" followed by the keyword `value` and the name of the variable into which the verdict is stored.
`all component.done` matches if no PTC is executing its behaviour.
`all component.done` matches if no PTC has been created.
`ptc.done` does not match for a PTC that has never been started, while `all component.done` can match at the same time because it considers only PTCs that have been started.
`any component.done` matches if the behaviour of at least one PTC has been stopped or the PTC has been killed.
`any component.done` IS unsuccessful if no PTC behaviour has been stopped and no PTC has been killed.
Stopping the behaviour of a non-alive test component removes that component from the test system.
Stopping the behaviour of an alive-type test component leaves the component alive in the test system.
The `done` operation matches both for a stopped non-alive test component and for a stopped alive-type test component.

When the `any from` component array notation is used with the `done` operation, each component of the referenced array IS checked individually for being stopped or killed, iterating from innermost to outermost dimension and from lowest to highest index within each dimension.
With the `any from` component array notation, the first component found being stopped or killed causes the `done` operation to succeed.

The index of the component matched by the `done` operation with `any from` MAY be assigned to an integer variable for a single-dimensional component array, or to an integer array or record of integer variable for a multi-dimensional component array.
The `done` operation SHALL be applied to PTCs only.
The ObjectReference of the `done` operation SHALL be of a component type.
The ObjectReference of the `done` operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The ComponentArrayRef of the `done` operation SHALL be a reference to a completely initialized component array.
The variable used in the value clause of the `done` operation for storing the final local verdict of a PTC SHALL be of type `verdicttype`.
The value clause of the `done` operation SHALL NOT be used in combination with `all component` or `any component`.
The index redirection of the `done` operation SHALL only be used when the operation is applied to an `any from` component array construct.
The type of the integer variable used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of the single-dimensional component array.
The size of the integer array or record of integer type used in the index redirection SHALL be exactly the same as the number of dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
The element type of the integer array or record of integer used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of all dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
If a variable referenced in the @index clause is a lazy or fuzzy variable, the expression assigned to that variable IS equal to the result produced by the `done` operation.
Later evaluation of a lazy or fuzzy variable referenced in the @index clause IS NOT a repeated invocation of the `done` operation.
The `@nodefault` modifier SHALL only be used with a stand-alone `done` statement.
The `killed` operation CAN be used to ascertain whether a different test component is alive or has been removed from the test system.
The `killed` operation CAN retrieve the final local verdict of a killed test component.
The final local verdict of a killed test component IS the value of its local verdict at the time when the test component was killed.

The `killed` operation has the syntax [ `@nodefault` ] ( ObjectReference | `any component` | `all component` | `any from` ComponentArrayRef ) "." `killed` [ "->" [ `value` ValueRef ] [ `@index` `value` ValueRef ] ].
The `killed` operation SHALL be used in the same manner as a receiving operation.
The `killed` operation SHALL NOT be used in a boolean expression.
The `killed` operation MAY be used to determine an alternative in an `alt` statement.
The `killed` operation MAY be used as a stand-alone statement in a behaviour description.
A stand-alone `killed` operation IS a shorthand for an `alt` statement with the `killed` operation as the only alternative.
If the `@nodefault` modifier is placed before a stand-alone `killed` operation, the implicit `alt` statement IS also qualified with the `@nodefault` modifier.

A `killed` operation applied to a non-alive test component matches if the component stopped (implicitly or explicitly) the execution of its behaviour or has been killed explicitly, i.e. it is equivalent to the `done` operation.
A `killed` operation applied to an alive-type test component matches only if the component has been killed using the `kill` operation.
A `killed` operation applied to an alive-type test component that has not been killed IS unsuccessful.
The execution of a `killed` operation does not change the state of the test component.
Consecutive `killed` operations applied to the same test component give the same result as long as the test component does not change its state.
`all component.killed` matches if all PTCs of the test case have ceased to exist.
`all component.killed` matches if no PTC has been created.
When a `killed` operation applied to a PTC matches, the final local verdict of that PTC MAY be retrieved and stored in a variable of type `verdicttype`.
Storing the final local verdict in a `killed` operation IS denoted by the symbol "->" followed by the keyword `value` and the name of the variable into which the verdict is stored.
`any component.killed` matches if at least one PTC has ceased to exist.
`any component.killed` IS unsuccessful if no PTC has ceased to exist.

When the `any from` component array notation is used with the `killed` operation, each component of the referenced array IS checked individually for being killed, iterating from innermost to outermost dimension and from lowest to highest index within each dimension.
With the `any from` component array notation, the first component found being killed causes the `killed` operation to succeed.

The index of the component matched by the `killed` operation with `any from` MAY be assigned to an integer variable for a single-dimensional component array, or to an integer array or record of integer variable for a multi-dimensional component array.
The `killed` operation SHALL be applied to PTCs only.
The ObjectReference of the `killed` operation SHALL be of a component type.
The ObjectReference of the `killed` operation SHALL NOT resolve to a template.
The ComponentArrayRef of the `killed` operation SHALL be a reference to a completely initialized component array.
The variable used in the value clause of the `killed` operation for storing the final local verdict of a PTC SHALL be of type `verdicttype`.
The value clause of the `killed` operation SHALL NOT be used in combination with `all component` or `any component`.
The index redirection of the `killed` operation SHALL only be used when the operation is applied to an `any from` component array construct.
The type of the integer variable used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of the single-dimensional component array.
The size of the integer array or record of integer type used in the index redirection SHALL be exactly the same as the number of dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
The element type of the integer array or record of integer used in the index redirection SHALL allow storing the highest index of all dimensions of the multi-dimensional component array.
If a variable referenced in the @index clause is a lazy or fuzzy variable, the expression assigned to that variable IS equal to the result produced by the `killed` operation.
Later evaluation of a lazy or fuzzy variable referenced in the @index clause IS NOT a repeated invocation of the `killed` operation.
The `@nodefault` modifier SHALL only be used with a stand-alone `killed` statement.
The keywords `any` and `all` MAY be used with configuration operations as indicated in table 21.
The `call` operation IS used to start a test behaviour on a test component and to wait until that test behaviour has terminated.

The `call` operation has the syntax ObjectReference "." `call` "(" (FunctionInstance | AltstepInstance) ["," SimpleExpression] ")" ["->" [`value` Ref] [`verdict` Ref]] [`catch` "(" `timeout` ")" StatementBlock] [`catch` "(" `stop` ")" StatementBlock].
The `call` operation IS blocking and implicitly uses a `start` operation on the test component.
The `call` operation SHALL wait until either the started test behaviour has terminated or the timeout duration has expired.
A `call` operation MAY have a timeout duration in seconds, given as a SimpleExpression additional parameter.
If no timeout duration is given, the `call` operation IS executed with an infinite timeout duration.
The actions taken by the `call` operation depend on whether the execution of the started test behaviour is complete or incomplete.
The execution of the started test behaviour IS complete when the started function terminates by executing a `return` statement or by reaching the end of its function body.
If the started test behaviour terminates for any reason other than executing a `return` statement or reaching the end of its function body, the execution IS incomplete.

If the execution is incomplete because the called component was stopped or killed and a `catch(stop)` clause is present, the StatementBlock of the `catch(stop)` clause SHALL be executed before the `call` operation terminates.
If the started test behaviour does not terminate within the given timeout duration and a `catch(timeout)` clause is present, the called component SHALL be implicitly stopped.

If the started test behaviour does not terminate within the given timeout duration and a `catch(timeout)` clause is present, the StatementBlock of the `catch(timeout)` clause SHALL be executed before the `call` operation terminates.
If the execution is incomplete and no matching `catch(stop)` or `catch(timeout)` clause handles it, the `call` operation SHALL end with a test case error.
The `create` operation SHALL NOT be used with the `any component` or `all component` keywords.
The `start` operation SHALL NOT be used with the `any component` or `all component` keywords.
`any component.running` and `all component.running` MAY be used in the MTC.
`any component.running` and `all component.running` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
`any component.running` IS true if any PTC is performing test behaviour.
`all component.running` IS true if all PTCs are performing test behaviour.
`any component.alive` and `all component.alive` MAY be used in the MTC.
`any component.alive` and `all component.alive` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
`any component.alive` IS true if any PTC is alive.
`all component.alive` IS true if all PTCs are alive.
`any component.done` and `all component.done` MAY be used in the MTC.
`any component.done` and `all component.done` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
`any component.done` IS true if any PTC has completed its execution.
`all component.done` IS true if all PTCs have completed their execution.
`any component.killed` and `all component.killed` MAY be used in the MTC.
`any component.killed` and `all component.killed` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
`any component.killed` IS true if any PTC has ceased to exist.
`all component.killed` IS true if all PTCs have ceased to exist.
`all component.stop` MAY be used in the MTC.
`all component.stop` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
The `stop` operation SHALL NOT be used with the `any component` keyword.
The `all component.stop` operation SHALL stop the behaviour on all PTCs.
`all component.kill` MAY be used in the MTC.
`all component.kill` SHALL NOT be used in a test component other than the MTC.
The `kill` operation SHALL NOT be used with the `any component` keyword.
The `all component.kill` operation SHALL kill all PTCs, so that they cease to exist.
The `any component` and `all component` keywords refer to PTCs only and do not consider the MTC.

After complete execution of the started test behaviour, the `out` and `inout` actual parameters of the called function or altstep instance SHALL be updated in the same manner as in a normal function or altstep invocation.
A `call` operation MAY have a redirect clause with a `value` clause that assigns the return value of the called function to a variable, if the called function has a return clause.
A `call` operation MAY have a redirect clause with a `verdict` clause that assigns the termination verdict of the called component to a variable.
In all cases of incomplete execution, the variables referenced in the `value` and `verdict` clauses and in `out` and `inout` actual parameters SHALL stay unchanged and no assignment SHALL be made.
A `call` operation SHALL NOT be applied to a test component that is not created alive and has already been started or called once, nor to a test component that has been killed.
The ObjectReference of a `call` operation SHALL be of a component type.
The function or altstep invoked in a `call` operation SHALL have a `runs on` clause referencing a component type to which the called component is compatible.
Every formal parameter of the function or altstep invoked in a `call` operation SHALL be of a component data type.
The return type of the function invoked in a `call` operation SHALL be a component data type.
The optional SimpleExpression giving the timeout duration of a `call` operation SHALL be of type `float`.
A `catch(timeout)` clause SHALL NOT be present in a `call` operation unless a timeout duration is given.
The variable in the `value` clause of a `call` operation SHALL be compatible with the return type of the invoked function.
The variable in the `verdict` clause of a `call` operation SHALL be of type `verdicttype`.
The TTCN-3 language IS supporting message-based unicast, multicast and broadcast communication.
The TTCN-3 language IS supporting procedure-based unicast, multicast and broadcast communication.
The TTCN-3 language CAN examine the top element of an incoming port queue.
The TTCN-3 language CAN control the access to a port by means of controlling operations.
Message-based communication IS communication based on an asynchronous message exchange.
The `send` operation IS non-blocking: processing in the sender SHALL continue immediately after the `send` operation occurs.
The `receive` operation IS blocking: the receiver is blocked on the `receive` operation until it processes the received message.
The `trigger` operation IS filtering messages that fulfil given matching criteria from the stream of received messages on a given incoming port.
When the `trigger` operation is executed, a message at the top of the port queue that does not fulfil the matching criteria IS removed from the port queue without any further action.
The `send` operation MAY be used at message-based ports.
The `send` operation SHALL NOT be used at procedure-based ports.
The `send` operation IS sending a message.
The `receive` operation MAY be used at message-based ports.
The `receive` operation SHALL NOT be used at procedure-based ports.
The `receive` operation IS receiving a message.
The `trigger` operation MAY be used at message-based ports.
The `trigger` operation SHALL NOT be used at procedure-based ports.
The `trigger` operation IS triggering on a message.
The `call` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `call` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `call` operation IS invoking a procedure call.
The `getcall` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `getcall` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `getcall` operation IS accepting a procedure call from a remote entity.
The `reply` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `reply` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `reply` operation IS replying to a procedure call from a remote entity.
The `raise` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `raise` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `raise` operation IS raising an exception to an accepted call.
The `getreply` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `getreply` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `getreply` operation IS handling the response from a previous call.
The `catch` operation MAY be used at procedure-based ports.
The `catch` operation SHALL NOT be used at message-based ports.
The `catch` operation IS catching an exception from the called entity.
The `check` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The `check` operation IS checking whether a message, call, exception or reply has been received at the top of the incoming port queue.
The `clear` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The `clear` operation IS clearing the port queue.
The `start` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The port `start` operation IS clearing the port queue and enabling sending and receiving at the port.
The `stop` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The port `stop` operation IS disabling sending at the port and disallowing receiving operations to match at the port.
The `halt` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The port `halt` operation IS disabling sending at the port and disallowing receiving operations to match new messages or calls.
The `checkstate` operation MAY be used at message-based ports and at procedure-based ports.
The `checkstate` operation IS checking the state of a port.
Procedure-based communication IS calling procedures in remote entities.
The TTCN-3 language IS supporting blocking procedure-based communication.
The TTCN-3 language IS supporting non-blocking procedure-based communication.
Blocking procedure-based communication IS blocking on the calling side and on the called side.
Non-blocking procedure-based communication IS blocking only on the called side.
A signature of a procedure used for non-blocking procedure-based communication SHALL be specified according to the rules in clause 13.
In blocking procedure-based communication, the caller IS calling a remote procedure in the callee by using the `call` operation.
In blocking procedure-based communication, the callee IS accepting the call by means of a `getcall` operation.
In blocking procedure-based communication, the callee IS reacting to an accepted call either with a `reply` operation answering the call or with a `raise` operation raising an exception.
In blocking procedure-based communication, the caller IS handling the reply or exception by using `getreply` or `catch` operations.
In non-blocking procedure-based communication, the caller IS continuing its execution after the `call` operation without waiting for a reply or exception.
In non-blocking procedure-based communication, the callee IS accepting the call by means of a `getcall` operation and executing the requested procedure.
In non-blocking procedure-based communication, if the execution of the requested procedure is not successful, the callee MAY raise an exception to inform the caller.
In non-blocking procedure-based communication, the caller MAY handle an exception by using a `catch` operation in an `alt` statement.
The TTCN-3 language IS supporting unicast, multicast and broadcast communication.
Unicast communication IS communication from one sender to one receiver.
Multicast communication IS communication from one sender to a list of receivers.
Broadcast communication IS communication from one sender to all receivers connected or mapped to the sender.
Unicast, multicast and broadcast communication IS related to port communication.
A unicast, multicast or broadcast communication operation CANNOT address a test component that is not connected to the specified port.
Unicast, multicast and broadcast communication MAY be used for mapped ports.
When unicast, multicast or broadcast communication is used via a mapped port, one, several or all entities within the SUT CAN be reached via the specified mapped port.
Communication operations such as `send` and `call` ARE used for the exchange of information among test components and between the SUT and test components.

A test component sends a message with the `send` operation, calls a procedure with the `call` operation, replies to an accepted call with the `reply` operation and raises an exception with the `raise` operation.
The `send`, `call`, `reply` and `raise` operations ARE collectively referred to as sending operations.

A test component receives a message with the `receive` operation, awaits a message with the `trigger` operation, accepts a procedure call with the `getcall` operation, receives a reply for a previously called procedure with the `getreply` operation and catches an exception with the `catch` operation.
The `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `getreply` and `catch` operations ARE collectively referred to as receiving operations.
A sending operation consists of a send part.
A blocking procedure-based `call` operation consists of a send part and a response and exception handling part.
The send part of a sending operation SHALL specify the port at which the operation takes place.
The send part of a sending operation SHALL define the message or procedure call to be transmitted.
The send part of a sending operation MAY contain an address part that uniquely identifies one or more communication partners to which the message, call, reply or exception is sent.
A sending operation SHALL contain the port name, the operation name and the value to be sent.
The address part (denoted by the `to` keyword) of a sending operation MAY be omitted.
The address part of a sending operation NEED NOT be specified except in one-to-many connections where unicast, multicast or broadcast communication requires the receiving entities to be identified.
In a one-to-many connection with unicast communication, the address part of a sending operation SHALL explicitly identify the one receiving entity.
In a one-to-many connection with multicast communication, the address part of a sending operation SHALL explicitly identify the set of receiving entities.
In a one-to-many connection with broadcast communication, the address part of a sending operation SHALL address all entities connected to the specified port.
A response and exception handling part IS only needed in procedure-based communication.
The response and exception handling part of a `call` operation MAY be omitted.

The response and exception handling part of a `call` operation SHALL be present when the called procedure returns a value or has `out` or `inout` parameters whose values are needed within the calling component.
The response and exception handling part of a `call` operation SHALL be present when the called procedure may raise exceptions that need to be handled by the calling component.
The response and exception handling part of a `call` operation uses `getreply` and `catch` operations.
A receiving operation consists of a receive part and an optional assignment part.
The receive part of a receiving operation SHALL specify the port at which the operation takes place.
The receive part of a receiving operation MAY contain a matching part that specifies the acceptable input matching the operation.
The receive part of a receiving operation MAY contain an address expression that uniquely identifies the communication partner in one-to-many connections.
A receiving operation SHALL contain the port name and the operation name.
The matching part of a receiving operation NEED NOT be present unless the content of the received communication is to be restricted.

The identification of the communication partner (`from` clause) in a receiving operation NEED NOT be specified except in one-to-many connections where the communication partner needs to be explicitly identified.
The assignment part of a receiving operation MAY be omitted.
For message-based ports, the assignment part of a receiving operation stores the received message.
For procedure-based ports, the assignment part of a receiving operation stores the `in` and `inout` parameters of an accepted call, the return value or the exception.
Strong typing IS NOT required for the message or parameter value assignment part of a receiving operation.
The variable used for storing a received message SHALL be type-compatible with the type of the incoming message.
The assignment part of a receiving operation MAY assign the sender address of a message, exception, reply or call to a variable.

Storing the sender address IS useful in one-to-many connections where the same message or call can be received from different components but the response has to be sent back to the original sending component.
For a receiving operation using `any from` on a port array, the assignment part MAY store the indices that identify the port instance where the receiving operation matched.
If a receiving operation is used as a stand-alone statement, the `@nodefault` modifier MAY be placed before it.
If a `@nodefault` modifier is placed before a stand-alone receiving operation, the implicit `alt` statement containing the operation as an alternative SHALL have the `@nodefault` modifier.
The `send` operation IS used to place a message on an outgoing message port.
The `send` operation has the syntax ObjectReference "." `send` "(" TemplateInstance ")" [ `to` Address ].
The Address in the `to` clause of a `send` operation MAY be an AddressRef, a list of AddressRef items or `all component`.
The `send` operation places a message on an outgoing message port.
The message of a `send` operation MAY be specified by referencing a defined template or as an in-line template.
The optional `to` clause of a `send` operation CAN determine unicast, multicast or broadcast communication.
The `to` clause of a `send` operation MAY be omitted in a one-to-one connection where unicast communication is used and the message receiver is uniquely determined by the test system structure.
A `send` operation uses unicast communication if the `to` clause addresses only one communication partner.
A `send` operation uses multicast communication if the `to` clause includes a list of communication partners.
A `send` operation uses broadcast communication if the `to` clause uses the `all component` keyword.
The TemplateInstance of a `send` operation, and all parts of it, SHALL have a specific value.
Matching mechanisms such as AnyValue SHALL NOT be used in the TemplateInstance of a `send` operation.
When the message of a `send` operation is defined in-line and the type of the message is ambiguous, the optional type part of the in-line template SHALL be used.
The `send` operation SHALL only be used on message-based ports.
The type of the template sent by a `send` operation SHALL be in the list of outgoing types of the port type definition.
The message-based communication operation 'send message' IS denoted by the keyword `send`.
The message-based communication operation 'receive message' IS denoted by the keyword `receive`.
The message-based communication operation 'trigger on message' IS denoted by the keyword `trigger`.
The message-based communication operation 'check message received' IS denoted by the keyword `check`.
A `send` operation SHALL contain a `to` clause in case of one-to-many connections.

Every AddressRef item in the `to` clause of a `send` operation SHALL be of type `address`, of a component type, or of the address type bound to the port type of the port instance referenced in the `send` operation.
No AddressRef in the `to` clause of a `send` operation SHALL contain the special value `null` at the time of the operation.
Applying a `send` operation to an unmapped or disconnected port SHALL cause a test case error.
The ObjectReference of a `send` operation SHALL be of a port type.
The TemplateInstance of a `send` operation SHALL be of a data type.
The `receive` operation IS the operation used to receive a message from an incoming message port queue.

The `receive` operation has the syntax [`@nodefault`] (ObjectReference | `any port` | `any from` PortArrayRef) "." `receive` ["(" TemplateInstance ")"] [`from` Address] ["->" [`value` (ValueRef | "(" {ValueRef [":=" [`@decoded` ["(" Expression ")"]] FieldOrTypeReference] [","]} ")")] [`sender` ValueRef] [`@index value` ValueRef]].
The Address in the `from` clause of a `receive` operation MAY be an AddressRef, a list of AddressRefs or `any component`.
The message to be received by a `receive` operation MAY be specified by referencing a defined template or MAY be defined as an in-line template.
The `receive` operation removes the top message from the associated incoming port queue if, and only if, that top message satisfies all the matching criteria associated with the `receive` operation.
If the match is not successful, the `receive` operation SHALL NOT remove the top message from the port queue.
If a `receive` operation used as an alternative of an `alt` statement is not successful, the execution of the `alt` statement SHALL continue with its next alternative.
The matching criteria of a `receive` operation are related to the type and value of the message to be received.
The type and value of the message to be received are determined by the argument of the `receive` operation, derived either from a defined template or from an in-line template.
The optional type part of the matching criteria of a `receive` operation SHALL be used to avoid any ambiguity of the type of the value being received.
Encoding attributes participate implicitly in matching by preventing the decoder from producing an abstract value from a received message encoded differently than specified by the attributes.
In the case of one-to-many connections, the `receive` operation MAY be restricted to a certain communication partner.

The restriction of a `receive` operation to a communication partner SHALL be denoted using the `from` keyword followed by an address or component reference, a list of address or component references, or `any component`.
A one-to-one connection is considered a simple case of a one-to-many connection, so the `from` clause MAY also be used for a `receive` operation on a one-to-one connection.
If the match is successful, the `receive` operation removes the received message from the port queue.
If the match is successful, the received value or parts of it CAN be stored in variables or formal parameters.
Storing the received message or parts of it is denoted by the symbol `->` followed by the keyword `value`.
When the keyword `value` is followed by the name of a variable or formal parameter, the whole received message SHALL be stored in that variable or formal parameter.
A variable or formal parameter following the keyword `value` SHALL be type compatible with the received message.
When the keyword `value` is followed by a parenthesized list, the whole received message and/or one or more parts of it CAN be stored.
For each element of a `value` redirect list that consists only of a variable or formal parameter name, the whole message SHALL be stored in that variable or formal parameter.
A variable or formal parameter that is a list element consisting only of a name in a `value` redirect list SHALL be of a type compatible with the type of the message.

Each assignment notation member of a `value` redirect list stores the value of the field or element of the received message referenced on the right hand side of `:=` in the variable or formal parameter on the left hand side.
A variable or formal parameter on the left hand side of an assignment notation member of a `value` redirect list SHALL be type compatible with the type of the referenced field or element.
When assigning individual fields of a received message, encoded payload fields MAY be decoded prior to assignment using the `@decoded` modifier.
When the `@decoded` modifier is used, the referenced field on the right hand side of the assignment SHALL be of the bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring or universal charstring type.
A field referenced with the `@decoded` modifier SHALL be decoded into a value of the same type as the variable on the left hand side of the assignment.
Failure of the decoding of a field referenced with the `@decoded` modifier SHALL cause a test case error.
If the referenced field is of the universal charstring type, the `@decoded` clause MAY contain an optional parameter defining the encoding format.
The encoding format parameter of the `@decoded` clause SHALL be of the charstring type.
The encoding format parameter of the `@decoded` clause SHALL contain one of the strings allowed for the `decvalue_unichar` function.
An encoding format parameter of the `@decoded` clause with a value not allowed for `decvalue_unichar` SHALL cause an error.
If the referenced field is not of the universal charstring type, the optional encoding format parameter of the `@decoded` clause SHALL NOT be present.
The `@decoded` clause is typically used together with the `decmatch` matching mechanism in the matching part of the receive statement.
A TTCN-3 tool CAN be optimized to call the decoder only once when a receiving statement contains both `decmatch` matching and `@decoded` assignment for the same payload field.
The component reference or address of the sender of a received message CAN be retrieved and stored.
Storing the sender of a received message is denoted by the keyword `sender`.
When the message is received on a connected port, only the component reference is stored in the variable following the `sender` keyword.
When the message is received on a connected port, the test system SHALL internally store the component name of the sender, if any, for use in logging.
A `receive` operation with no argument for the type and value matching criteria SHALL remove the message on the top of the incoming port queue, if any, if all other matching criteria are fulfilled.
The `any port` keywords MAY be used with the `receive` operation to receive a message on any port.
The `any from` PortArrayRef construct MAY be used with the `receive` operation to receive a message on any port of a specific port array.
The PortArrayRef in an `any from` PortArrayRef construct SHALL be a reference to a port array identifier.
The index of the port in a single-dimensional port array at which the `receive` operation was successful MAY be stored in a variable of type integer.
The index of the successful port in a multi-dimensional port array MAY be stored in an integer array or record of integer variable.
When checking a port array for matching messages, the port indices are iterated from lowest to highest.
If the port array is multi-dimensional, the ports are iterated from innermost to outermost array dimension, from lowest to highest index for each dimension (e.g. [0][0], [0][1], [1][0], [1][1]).
The first port of the port array that matches all the criteria causes the `receive` operation to be successful, even if other ports in the array would also meet the criteria.
The `receive` operation CAN be used as a stand-alone statement in a behaviour description.
A stand-alone `receive` operation is shorthand for an `alt` statement with the `receive` operation as the only alternative.
When the message is defined in-line, the optional type part SHALL be present whenever the type of the message being received is ambiguous.
The `receive` operation SHALL only be used on message-based ports.
The type of the value to be received by a `receive` operation SHALL be included in the list of incoming types of the port type definition.
A `receive` operation SHALL NOT bind incoming values to the terms of the expression or to the template.
A `receive` operation without an argument (receive any message) SHALL NOT contain a `value` clause.
A type mismatch at storing the received value or parts of the received value SHALL cause an error.
A type mismatch at storing the sender SHALL cause an error.

A type mismatch error can happen if the types in the receive part are not compatible with the types in the assignment part, or if the `from` clause is missing but the type of the sender can be determined and is not type compatible with the type in the `sender` clause.
Every AddressRef in the `from` clause of a `receive` operation SHALL be of type `address`, of a component type, or of the address type bound to the port type of the referenced port.
